#5700. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. #5699. AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have packaged agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 packaged agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”

#5698. EXCLUSIVE: ‘The Wolves of Real Estate’ Director Reveals the Unanswered Questions Behind the Alexander Brothers’ Downfall

Before their names became synonymous with a federal sex-trafficking case, Tal and Oren Alexander built careers selling some of the country’s most expensive homes.

Now, a documentary examining the brothers and their crimes is raising questions about the role wealth, professional prestige, and exclusive social circles played in giving them access to women.

Peacock’s three-part series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” examines the rise and downfall of Tal, Oren, and their brother Alon, tracing a story that stretched from luxury properties and lavish parties to a Manhattan courtroom.

All three were convicted of federal sex offenses, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, on March 9. On Oct. 27, each was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Emma Schwartz, director of “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” says the brothers’ status helped draw women into their orbit, while cautioning against assuming that every allegation involved their professional lives.

“Testimony at trial made clear that the brothers’ wealth and status was one of the reasons they were able to attract so many women,” Schwartz says.

“But many of the allegations we heard about did not involve their jobs or work.”

Tal and Oren rose to prominence at Douglas Elliman before leaving in 2022 to co-found luxury brokerage Official.

Their résumés included the $238 million Manhattan penthouse transaction at 220 Central Park South in 2019, which set a U.S. residential sale record at the time. Alon, Oren’s twin, worked in the family’s private security business.

Prosecutors described a scheme in which the brothers used their money and connections, including Tal and Oren’s standing in ultraluxury real estate, to facilitate sexual assaults.

Women were enticed with trips, accommodations, and exclusive experiences, according to the government’s account of the evidence.

Yet the criminal proceedings were not primarily an examination of the brokerage business, Schwartz explains.

“One of the interesting things about the criminal trial was how little it focused on the brothers’ professional lives,” Schwartz says.

Only one Douglas Elliman agent testified, according to the interview responses, with the government seeking information about a summer lease in the Hamptons.

Nevertheless, some testimony revealed an overlap between the properties associated with the brothers’ business image and the places where women said they were assaulted.

“For instance, the house that two women testified at trial that they were raped and trafficked to, was featured in a business video for the brothers,” Schwartz says.

Another woman testified that the possibility of making a professional connection had interested her in attending a party to which the brothers had invited her friend, according to Schwartz.

Those accounts illustrate how professional opportunity and social access could intersect. They do not, on their own, establish that the brothers systematically used access to clients’ listings to commit crimes.

Questions about what others knew also remain central to the story.

“One of the biggest questions so many have is who knew what about the brothers’ behavior?” Schwartz says.

The interview responses point to an email from an Elliman official, discussed in the documentary and presented at trial, as evidence that at least some people knew about the brothers’ playboy lifestyle.

But Schwartz distinguishes that awareness from knowledge of sexual violence.

“We also know from reporters at The Real Deal that there had been rumors about the brothers’ alleged behavior circulating in the industry for years before the lawsuits came out,” Schwartz says.

Rumors, awareness of partying, and evidence that a particular person knew about a crime are different matters. The responses do not establish criminal wrongdoing by the brokerage or its other employees.

For Schwartz, another striking aspect of the trial was the difficulty women described in acknowledging and reporting their experiences.

“One of the striking things about the trial was how so many of the women said they had been ashamed and too afraid to report what happened to them,” Schwartz says.

Some took months or years to describe what happened as rape or sexual assault, according to the interview responses.

That hesitation is a significant part of the documentary’s larger story: the barriers women faced in coming forward, even as the brothers maintained wealth and social standing.

“This all raises an important issue about sexual assault cases: women often take a long time, sometimes years, before they are ready to speak about what happened,” Schwartz says.

The civil justice system also played a role. New York’s Adult Survivors Act created a temporary window allowing adults to bring certain sexual-assault claims that would otherwise have been barred by expired filing deadlines. That window ran from Nov. 24, 2022 through Nov. 24, 2023.

Schwartz credits that law with allowing the first two women to file their civil claims, helping set in motion the public scrutiny that followed.

“This is a story about why speaking up matters,” Schwartz says.

“It took just two women filing lawsuits, amplified by the media to open the floodgates for dozens of women to come forward.”

Asked whether the case reveals something broader about luxury brokerages, Schwartz resists drawing a sweeping conclusion about the entire industry.

“It’s really hard to know how much anyone can generalize from the brothers to the industry more broadly.”

The hope, instead, is that the women’s accounts will help others feel able to share their own experiences.

“The women and people who spoke for our documentary did so in hopes that sharing their experience would encourage others to speak up and not feel the shame they did.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5697. Meta acquires AI coding startup Conductor, whose app runs several coding agents at once

Meta Platforms Inc. has acquired artificial intelligence coding startup Conductor in a deal first reported today by Axios.

Conductor confirmed it’s joining Meta in a post on its website. Terms were not disclosed.

The company’s software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, and then review and merge what they produce. Supported agents include Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Cursor, and users pay for them through their own subscriptions and keys.

The desktop app runs on Macs. A hosted version, Conductor Cloud, puts agents in sandboxed virtual machines where they can keep working for hours, and users can check on them from an iPhone app.

Engineers at Meta were using Conductor well before the deal. When the startup announced its Series A in March, it named Meta, Google LLC and Spotify Technology SA among the companies with dozens of engineers on the product. Conductor now says on its website that more than 100,000 people use it.

People familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team’s speed at shipping products to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools. The acquisition follows two Meta model releases last month that both pitched coding as a strength.

On Oct. 15, Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights version of its Muse Spark model aimed at coding and long-running agent work. Meta’s more capable Muse Wonder models stay closed inside its own Muse Code terminal and application programming interface.

The Conductor deal landed the same day OpenAI said it plans to acquire developer tools startup Pierre Computer. OpenAI had already announced plans in June to buy Ona, which runs coding agents in cloud sandboxes.

Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027, when the team expects to release a new interface it has not yet described. New models and critical bug fixes stop arriving at that point, and Conductor will delete the app’s user data. The company said it has never sold Conductor user data or trained models on it, and does not plan to.

Chief Executive Charlie Holtz and Chief Technology Officer Jackson de Campos founded the company, formally Melty Inc., in 2024. Conductor raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix. Y Combinator and the founders of Notion and Linear are also backers.

#5696. JD Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Rout After Mortgage Rates Soared

Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans' election losses on the Iran conflict and rising prices.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance said in a post on X, hours after Democrats shellacked Republicans in the midterm elections, flipping almost three dozen seats in the House and Senate to win control of both chambers.

Vance noted that polling found the war in Iran and cost of living and inflation concerns were the top items on voters' minds heading into Election Day.

Those were among the top reasons that many of the voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to a second term in 2024, with majorities in both chambers of Congress, voted in Democrats on Tuesday, Vance said.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in the post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said.

Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Mortgage rates reached a three-year high of 7.4% in the run-up to the election, before pulling back to 7.24% last week, according to Freddie Mac. The surge has been driven by inflation concerns and rising oil prices in the wake of Trump's Iran war, which also forced the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark rate in September.

Both Democrats and Republicans have promised their own affordability agendas for the coming months. But in swing states that turned against Trump, including Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine, housing affordability was at the top of voters' minds. So, too, have many young voters worried that homeownership is rising out of reach.

Most markers of inflation show many costs have risen sharply this year. Gas prices often embody Americans' concerns, and AAA reports the national average price for gas is $4.12 a gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago.

Trump, for his part, continued defending his economic record on Tuesday, telling media outlets that night that he would accept the election results and might seek common ground with Democrats.

But then he also posted an image of a red hat with the word "veto" on it, before celebrating the rise of the Dow the next morning following the results.

"Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years," he posted to Truth Social on Wednesday. "Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!"

And yet, the war in Iran and its resultant rise in oil prices and other costs hamstrung efforts to improve affordability. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates earlier this year, and kept them steady in its most recent meeting. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee in recent months show that leaders are worried that inflation is stickier than expected and that the conflict with Iran will continue to drive up costs.

Vance said in his post that it was "sound" political advice to call for a diplomatic solution to the Iran conflict. He also indicated that he could be open for change to the controversial immigration enforcement policies that have deeply affected the housing market and home construction.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance," Vance said in the post. "But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you."

Meanwhile, Democratic leaders said in a press conference on Wednesday that they would focus on affordability in the coming term.

New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, repeatedly avoided discussing Trump. Instead, he said his focus was on "affordability and accountability."

"We know we have to undertake, with the seriousness of purpose, a relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Later he added, "We have been focused, relentlessly, on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living."

Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark, who is currently minority whip but stands as a contender to become House majority leader, said that could include efforts to roll back the president's tariffs, which have driven up the cost of many homebuilding materials and household goods.

Jeffries said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out a clear plan for what to do next. But neither he nor Sen. Chuck Schumer had heard directly from Trump on Wednesday.

The National Association of Realtors®, in a Wednesday statement, called for more progress on housing.

“Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership," NAR said. "Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle."

RPAC-supported candidates won in at least 325 races, and a number of ballot initiatives this year involved housing-related issues. NAR also noted the bipartisanship of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, the housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes. Congress passed it this summer with large majorities from both parties.

"We will continue building on that momentum, working with REALTOR® champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership," NAR said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5695. The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save

Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027, according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise.

But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention.

“Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey, president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL.

By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home’s condition and value without draining your savings.

There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly.

“Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains.

Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal.

If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel.

“Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey.

A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape.

“If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains.

Dmitri Popescu, general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle, echoes Dausey’s thoughts.

“Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains.

Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer.

“Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey.

An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait.

“Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey.

These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait:

Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics?

“Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad, chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA.

Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue.

“They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says.

If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money.

“Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains.

Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away.

Keith Ostendorf, project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA, recommends phasing.

“Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.

#5694. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5693. Zillow Says Lawsuits in the Past, ‘Not Obvious’ How Market Recovers

Real estate’s biggest name is struggling, just like everyone else, but company leadership is promising that it—and the industry—have ways to hang on amid a tech revolution, a sluggish market and legal woes the company claims are in the past now.

Speaking to investors after reporting earnings for Q3 2026, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business,” with CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann adding that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

Zillow’s report comes as mortgage rates remain elevated from earlier this year and existing home sales are on track to come in around 4 million—down more than 20% from pre-pandemic norms. The company’s stock fell sharply, down around 17% in after-hours trading.

The company still faces a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Democratic lawmakers previously offered pointed criticism of some of Zillow’s business practices, which are also used by at least some other portals, as the party made big gains in the midterms yesterday.

On the tech side, Zillow said it has not seen major impacts from increased use of AI by consumers, or Google’s ongoing push into residential real estate.

“(Google’s program) is very different than a ‘Preferred’ connection and an integrated transaction and helping agents grow their business that way. So we haven’t seen any impact from it today, even though it’s supposedly live nationwide,” Wacksman said.

As the company previously announced, agent partners are all being transitioned from other programs to the company’s Zillow Preferred service, which executives said is integrated with Zillow Home Loans.

The transition is expected to be fully implemented by the first half of 2027, and 75% complete by the end of this year.

Zillow’s residential for-sale revenue was down 4% year-over-year, $419 million in Q3 2026 compared to $435 million in Q3 2025. On the other hand, mortgage revenue grew 32%, and the company touted durable rental income, up 26% from the same period last year.

Overall revenue came in up 7% from last year at $724 million, with the lawsuit payment—$165 million after insurance covered part of the settlement—dinging the top—line. Outlook for Q4—historically the slowest for real estate—was $635 to $665 million, roughly the same as last year’s reported $654 million.

Late last year, Zillow was targeted by a high-profile class-action firm with claims from recent homebuyers focused on those “lead diversion” and loan referral practices. A judge initially threw that lawsuit out (though plaintiffs are seeking to revive it).

The company also agreed last week to pay $212.5 million to settle a lawsuit over its long-shuttered iBuying business, something the company said it was happy to put behind it.

“I think we’ve been pretty consistent and transparent to the degree we could be, that we didn’t expect these cases to impact business. And I think as you’re seeing them resolve, get settled, move on, you’re seeing that come to light. They’re not impacting our business,” Wacksman said.

As far as the macro picture, Hofmann said that without any sign of a market rebound, “its our job (to) just keep driving on the underlying structural growth drivers we have,” including software and rentals that are not rate dependent.

“We’re also fortunate in that the business has diversified pretty rapidly over the last four or five years,” he said.

Addressing the use of agentic AI and potential changes in how consumers search for homes, Wacksman and Hofmann both promised that Zillow’s model was built to thrive in this new environment.

“We see the human experiences remaining human,” Wacksman said. “The dreaming and shopping part is the part you want to do and the transaction part is the part you need to do, and Zillow is the best place to do both those things…and then our ability to make the professional’s job easier so they can serve the customer better is where we’re focused, and why we are so confident in the strategy.”

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5691. Meghan Trainor Lists $18 Million Encino Mansion Formerly Owned by Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner

Meghan Trainor is saying goodbye to her sprawling Encino, CA, mansion, and has listed it for $17,995,000.

Although the manse is only 6 years old, it's already been home to a number of celebrity residents.

The “All About That Bass” singer and her husband, “Spy Kids” actor Daryl Sabara, purchased the abode in 2024 for $17,125,000. Previously, the dwelling belonged to music producer Zedd, who had listed the home for just under $19 million in January of that year.

The “Clarity” producer snapped up the six-bedroom, 12-bathroom property for $15.2 million in September 2021 from Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner.

The Jonas Brothers rocker and “Game of Thrones” star were the original owners, having bought the home for $14.1 million when it was built in 2019.

Spanning about 14,779 square feet, the home was designed by "distinguished” architect Jae Omar and sits on a near-acre of land in the exclusive Royal Oaks enclave.

A lavish two-story entrance creates an “incredible indoor/outdoor feel,” according to the listing, which notes that the compound is “for the most discerning buyer.”

With an impressive scale and an open-concept flow, the home is well-suited for hosting large gatherings as well as intimate dinners.

A generously sized great room with wall-to-wall sliding doors opens the home to an idyllic courtyard, while a built-in bar and a soothing fireplace keep things cozy.

The chef's kitchen has a sleek aesthetic, with modern cabinetry and countertops and a picture-frame window located above one of the two sinks. It’s also equipped with Miele appliances and a discreet refrigerator.

An oversized island seats seven, creating a perfect spot for families to spend quality time together.

There’s even a separate catering kitchen for more involved occasions.

Young children—like Trainor and Sabara’s three little ones, Riley Thomas, Barry Bruce, and Mikey Moon—could never be bored here. The property also includes an office space, a professional music studio with a vocal booth, and a fitness center with a steam shower.

The second floor includes yet another family room and five en suite bedrooms.

In its own wing, the primary suite has a sitting area, wet bar, and multiple patios. The spalike bathroom is impossibly luxurious, with an oversized walk-in shower and a soaking tub.

According to the listing, the primary suite’s two walk-in closets are “reminiscent of a luxury boutique.”

The backyard is yet another destination for a young family to enjoy, with “park-like” grounds that can be used for lounging, entertaining, and play.

Outdoor amenities include a kitchen and barbecue, a putting green, a fire pit, and a projection screen. “Enchanting” lighting and a robust sound system add to the magic.

The sparkling pool has a spa and runs alongside a separate guest structure that has a pub with a billiard room and fish tank. On the second floor is a fully decked-out screening room.

The property comes with a four-car garage, a security room with high-tech cameras throughout, and a Control4 smart home system.

This is the second Encino property Trainor has had on the market this year.

#5690. Cyber ups and downs: Datadog falls 14% on outlook tied to one customer as Rapid7 jumps and Fastly slides

Datadog Inc., Rapid7 Inc. and Fastly Inc. all beat Wall Street’s third-quarter forecasts today, but Rapid7 was the only one of the three to see its shares rise.

A cautious outlook tied to one large customer knocked about 14% off Datadog’s stock in regular trading. Rapid7 jumped 18% after hours on results that came despite a decline in revenue.

For its third quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Datadog reported adjusted earnings of 81 cents per share, up from 55 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 64 cents per share on revenue of $1.14 billion.

Unadjusted net income climbed to $118.3 million from $33.9 million, and the adjusted operating margin widened five points to 28%. Billings in the quarter rose 30% to $1.16 billion, Chief Financial Officer David Obstler said on the earnings call, with remaining performance obligations up 38% at $3.85 billion. Free cash flow came to $251 million.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Olivier Pomel told analysts that more than 850 artificial intelligence companies now use Datadog, roughly 100 more than at the end of June. Adoption is strong across the platform as customers scale “their digital operations and use of AI,” he said in the earnings release. Customers worth $100,000 or more a year in recurring revenue rose 20% to about 4,860.

Full-year guidance went up. Datadog now expects 2026 revenue of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion, against the $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion it projected in August, and adjusted earnings of $2.73 to $2.75 per share. Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are forecast at 69 to 71 cents per share.

Revenue for the fourth quarter is guided at $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly what analysts had expected, with the top of the range only about $3 million above third-quarter revenue. The forecast assumes Datadog’s largest customer, an AI provider the company has not named, spends no more than its contractual minimum, according to Obstler.

Usage on that account dropped in the third quarter while staying above the floor. Excluding it, implied fourth-quarter growth is in the low- to mid-30% range. Early renewals with some large AI customers, signed at higher commitments in return for better pricing, are also holding back near-term revenue.

The roughly 14% drop today made it two straight quarters in which a beat failed to hold up the stock. Datadog shares closed 19% lower in August, the day the company disclosed the customer’s planned cutback.

In Rapid7’s third quarter, also ended Sept. 30, the cybersecurity company posted adjusted earnings of 60 cents per share, up from 57 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $212.4 million, down 2.5% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 46 cents per share on revenue of $209 million.

Annualized recurring revenue slipped 2.2%, to $819.7 million, ahead of the roughly $812 million the company had guided to in August. Adjusted operating income rose to $46.2 million from $36.9 million. Unadjusted net income fell to $3.5 million from $9.8 million after $10 million in restructuring costs from the 12% workforce cut announced in August and a $5.5 million write-down on a strategic equity investment.

Rapid7 demonstrated its Agentic SOC at Black Hat USA in August, using AI agents to speed up investigations while leaving high-impact decisions to analysts. Wael Mohamed, who took over as CEO in June, said the core business “is becoming more stable” and that “one quarter of stability is just a start.” Rapid7 is “not declaring victory,” he added.

The company’s full-year adjusted earnings forecast moved to $1.94 to $1.96 per share, well above the $1.78 to $1.83 it gave three months ago. Revenue guidance edged up to $841 million to $843 million. For the fourth quarter, Rapid7 sees revenue of $208 million to $210 million, down 3% to 4% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of 53 to 55 cents per share.

The stock climbed about 18% in extended trading.

Edge cloud platform provider Fastly reported adjusted earnings of 17 cents per share for its third quarter, up from 7 cents a year earlier, on record revenue of $190.2 million, up 20% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 12 cents per share on revenue of $187.9 million.

Most of Fastly’s revenue still comes from network services, which grew 16%, to $138 million. Security sales rose twice as fast, to $44.7 million, in a quarter when the company also launched AI Firewall to block prompt injection and other attacks before they reach a model. Trailing-12-month net retention was its highest since 2022, at 119%. The top 10 customers now account for 39% of revenue, up from 32% a year ago.

Fourth-quarter revenue is forecast at $198 million to $202 million, ahead of the $197 million analysts had modeled. Full-year revenue guidance moved up to $744 million to $748 million from $732 million to $746 million in August. Adjusted earnings for 2026 are now expected at 61 to 63 cents per share. None of that stopped Fastly shares from falling about 14% after the bell.

#5689. Former Landsea Homes President and COO Mike Forsum to Lead New Land Finance Platform

Home building industry veteran Mike Forsum has been tapped to lead a new land finance platform aimed at providing public and private home builders and developers with more flexible capital options.

Wafra, a New York-based global alternative investment manager, and Hunt Cos., a privately held real estate and investment company, have launched Strata Land Partners, with Forsum serving as CEO.

The platform has launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and is designed to serve as a long-term capital partner for builders navigating land investment and development in an uncertain housing market.

Forsum brings more than 40 years of home building industry experience to the venture. Most recently, he served as president and chief operating officer of Landsea Homes. His experience navigating builders’ operational challenges and investment decisions will help shape Strata’s approach.

“Strata was built by builders, for builders,” Forsum said. “Having spent my career in home building, it is apparent that there is significant demand for a strategic capital partner that understands the industry’s operational nuances and thoughtfully supports builders in achieving their goals.”

He added that the platform’s goal is to “bridge that gap and play our part in building the new homes this country needs.”

Strata enters the market as builders look for ways to manage land exposure and capital requirements. According to the announcement, the platform will focus on tailored financing solutions that allow builders and developers to navigate changing market conditions while advancing residential projects.

Ryan Brenner, managing director and head of alternative real estate at Wafra, said Strata is also intended to help address the nation’s structural housing shortage by giving builders another source of capital to support new-home development.

For Hunt Cos., the partnership combines flexible capital with an operating team experienced in residential development.

“Strata brings together an experienced operating team and flexible capital to address a critical need in residential development,” said Chris Hunt, CEO of Hunt Cos. “We look forward to supporting the platform as it builds lasting relationships with home builders and developers nationwide.”

Leah Draffen is a senior editor for Zonda's Builder and Multifamily Executive magazines. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5688. Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress

Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed.

The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump, who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence."

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

"If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula, CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com.

Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas, Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend.

Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in.

Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act.

That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts. But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level.

In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act, with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines.

Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move.

Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence.

The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding."

While data centers affect property taxes, the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open.

Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers.

"Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far."

The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions.

Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas.

It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says.

"That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5687. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

#5686. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

#5685. Kylie Kelce Reveals the One Thing That Makes Someone the Perfect Houseguest

Kylie Kelce has revealed what a visitor needs to do to be the perfect guest in their home—and it has to do with impressing her and her NFL-star husband Jason Kelce's daughters.

On a recent episode of her podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," the mom of four revealed that their daughters— Finnley, 18 months, Bennett, 3, Elliotte, 5, and Wyatt, 7—love having guests read to them.

“I know one way to my girls’ hearts, and really kids, I always tell people you don’t need to bring gifts when you come to our house. If you come in, you sit down, you offer to read our girls a book, they will be like forever," she revealed.

Kelce added, “Like genuinely, we have obviously family [that] will come and they’ll bring this and they’ll bring that, but if when you come and you sit down, you read a book, I think it’s one of the best ways to connect with kids.”

The glimpse of her houseguest request came just days after she defended her and her spouse's decision to snap up multiple Philadelphia properties right next to each other.

In an episode of her podcast, which featured guest Nikki Glaser, Kelce, 34, and the comedian chatted about hate comments.

"Do you ever get in the comments? Do you ever get feisty?” Glaser asked.

In her reply, Kelce detailed an Instagram account that frequently posts information about their real estate.

“One of the ones that I did it—which was not to a person so it doesn’t really feel as aggressive—was like ‘Celeb Homes.’ They put a bird’s-eye view of where we live with our children, and they were trying to give details of our property," she said.

The account then revealed that the Kelce family had also purchased the home "next door."

She then told the comedian, "I think I typed ‘get f---ed.’ And then when I tried to post it, it wouldn’t let me. Why? I want to tell people to get f---ed."

Her admission came after she offered a glimpse of the family's childcare arrangements during an appearance on an episode of "IMO with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson." She explained that she and the former Philadelphia Eagles star prefer to keep their relatives closely involved in raising their children.

The couple have built a support system that allows them to balance their professional commitments with family life.

A major part of that arrangement involves Kelce's parents, Lisa and Ed McDevitt, who live just 15 minutes from the family's Philadelphia-area home.

Kelce explained that her parents regularly help care for the girls, making it possible for her and Jason to navigate their busy schedules without relying on round-the-clock childcare.

Although the couple do employ a nanny, Kelce revealed that the arrangement is limited to traditional working hours rather than having someone live in their home.

“My husband and I have very busy schedules. We don’t necessarily want a live-in nanny or someone who’s going to be raising our kids void of us. That feels weird. So we do a lot with my parents every chance we get. We do things with Jason’s parents. We find that those are the values that we were raised with that we want our kids to have, not just because we tell them that, but because we live it," she explained.

The decision, she explained, reflects their desire to remain actively involved in their daughters' everyday lives.

Rather than bringing in someone to provide full-time care, the Kelces turn to their extended family for additional support.

Kelce said maintaining those close family relationships is particularly important because she wants her daughters to grow up with the same values that shaped her and Jason's childhoods.

She also emphasized how grateful she is for the nanny who helps the family during the workday, acknowledging that the additional support is essential to managing their responsibilities.

However, the couple's approach to childcare goes beyond convenience.

For Kelce, living close to her parents has been a priority, and she admitted that the thought of settling somewhere far from her family has never appealed to her.

“We couldn’t do it without my parents. My parents live 15 minutes from us, and they have helped us in every way imaginable," she said.

The Pennsylvania native explained that remaining in the area where she grew up has allowed her to preserve those relationships while raising her own family.

That connection to her hometown has also influenced the kind of upbringing she hopes to provide her daughters.

Kelce wants the girls to become familiar with the places that shaped her childhood, from local businesses to the community organizations that continue to play a role in her life.

She believes that growing up with those personal connections can help children develop a stronger sense of responsibility toward the communities around them.

Her own involvement with the Eagles Autism Foundation is one example of how she has maintained those local ties.

For Kelce, the opportunity to contribute to the community where she was raised is another benefit of remaining close to home.

“Now, granted, we do have a nanny. I always give a shoutout because we couldn’t do it without her, but we have her during regular work hours and really nothing outside of that," she added.

#5684. Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep

Shares of Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. closed higher today following Democrats’ resounding midterm victory.

Amazon jumped 8.3% at one point and ended the trading session 6.1% higher than Tuesday. Microsoft gained nearly 6.7% while Alphabet and Google rose by about 3.1% and 1.4%, respectively. Multiple industry analysts tied the stock gains to the companies’ artificial intelligence buildout.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on a campaign that emphasized data center restrictions. Furthermore, voters approved 40 ballot measures focused on blocking or limiting AI infrastructure projects. Bloomberg cited Robert Pavlik, a senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, as saying that tech giants’ shares jumped because investors believe a data center slowdown could improve their finances.

Amazon, Meta and Google have become cash-flow-negative in recent months because of their steep infrastructure investments. Last Wednesday, the search giant reported a negative cash flow that exceeded the consensus estimate by about $6.4 billion. Google’s stock price plummeted 10% in after-hours trading even though its cloud revenue more than doubled.

Needham & Co., B. ‌Riley ⁠Wealth and prominent tech industry analyst Ben Thompson highlighted another possible contributor to the stock rally. New restrictions on AI projects would make computing infrastructure more scarce, which would boost the value of existing data centers. That would benefit the tech giants that logged share price gains today.

Thompson noted that neoclouds, or emerging AI-focused cloud providers, may also benefit in certain respects. Developments for which they have already secured regulatory permission could become more valuable. At the same time, they may find it more difficult to finance new sites.

That dynamic weighed on chip stocks today. Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. both shed more than 3% of their value, while Broadcom Inc. declined 2%. SK hynix Inc., the world’s largest supplier of HBM memory for graphics cards, dropped by more than 5%. One notable exception was Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which ended the trading day about 1% higher.

Thompson noted that the midterms could also affect the AI industry in other ways. He pointed out that a stricter regulatory environment may give space-based data centers a boost. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, in turn, could see their hardware costs decline if new restrictions are placed on frontier model training. Such a development may ease their path to profitability.

Last month, Meta announced plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares to finance new data centers. On Monday, Oracle Corp. filed to issue $20 billion worth of bonds and shares in connection with its own AI buildout. It’s currently unclear how the midterm results will affect those initiatives and other large-scale data center projects currently underway.

#5683. The Home Depot Foundation Expands Veteran Housing Commitment to $1 Billion

The Home Depot Foundation is increasing its total commitment to veteran causes to $1 billion through 2032, expanding investments in programs designed to address veteran homelessness, housing insecurity, and home accessibility.

Since 2011, the foundation says it has invested more than $650 million in veteran causes and helped improve more than 70,000 veteran homes and facilities. Its latest commitment will combine established housing programs with efforts to test and scale new approaches to veteran housing.

“We believe every veteran deserves a safe place to call home,” said Erin Izen, executive director of The Home Depot Foundation. “Our $1 billion commitment supports the partnerships and solutions needed to help more veterans move from uncertainty to long-term stability.”

Among the initiatives receiving support are programs designed to remove barriers to rental housing. The Landlords, Organizations, and Veterans Engagement (LOVE) Fund, with Open Doors Atlanta, and the U.S. VETS Master Lease Program aim to speed veteran housing placements by addressing costs such as security deposits and application fees or by leasing units directly from property owners.

The foundation is also investing in homelessness prevention and permanent supportive housing through organizations including Operation Homefront and Community Solutions. Additional funding will explore alternative housing approaches, including modular homes from Purple Heart Homes for senior veterans and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The announcement coincides with the foundation’s annual Celebration of Service. This fall, Team Depot, The Home Depot’s associate volunteer force, is expected to complete hundreds of projects benefiting veterans across all 50 states and three U.S. territories.

One recent project brought The Home Depot Foundation, Team Depot, and Purple Heart Homes together to construct a fully accessible modular home on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for James “Jim” Taylor, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who previously experienced homelessness. The home was subsequently transported to Virginia, where a dedication is planned.

#5682. LGI Homes Posts Q3 Gains Despite Slower Sales Activity

LGI Homes posted year-over-year gains in closings, revenue, and earnings during the third quarter, even as affordability pressures continued to weigh on buyer demand and slow sales activity.

The Texas-based builder delivered 1,222 homes during the quarter, up 10.4% from a year earlier, including 33 currently and previously leased homes. Its 1,189 new-home closings generated $437.5 million in home building revenue, an increase of 10.3% year over year. Total revenue increased 10.2% to $444.5 million.

“We delivered strong third quarter financial results, generating year-over-year growth in closings, revenue, and earnings while maintaining strong profitability, expanding our community count, and further strengthening our balance sheet,” chairman and CEO Eric Lipar said.

Net income increased to $24.6 million from $19.7 million in the prior-year quarter, while diluted earnings per share increased to $1.05 from $0.85.

Home building gross margin was 20.2% in the third quarter, while adjusted home building gross margin was 23.7%. Both were above the midpoint of LGI Homes’ previous guidance ranges and improved 40 basis points sequentially.

Lipar attributed the margin performance in part to the company’s predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet land position and its approach to balancing affordability and profitability.

“Our teams also did an excellent job managing costs. SG&A expenses declined on an absolute-dollar basis, and SG&A as a percentage of total revenues improved 180 basis points year over year,” he said.

The builder also continued expanding its footprint, ending the third quarter with 151 active communities, an increase of 7.1% from the prior-year period.

Despite stronger closings and revenue, LGI Homes said affordability pressure contributed to slower sales activity during the quarter.

Through the first nine months of 2026, net orders totaled 2,869, compared with 4,098 during the same period in 2025. The cancellation rate increased to 48.9% from 28.1%, while ending backlog declined to 685 homes from 1,305 a year earlier.

The trend marks a reversal from the beginning of the year, when LGI Homes ended the first quarter with 1,699 homes in backlog, up 63.4% year over year. At the time, management pointed to improving sales activity and a growing backlog as evidence of steady demand heading into the spring selling season.

By the third quarter, however, affordability had become a more significant headwind.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership and are leaning into our proven sales and marketing strategies to improve sales pace while maintaining our disciplined approach to balancing affordability and profitability,” Lipar said.

Based on its year-to-date results and current market conditions, LGI Homes narrowed its full-year closing guidance and now expects to deliver between 4,600 and 4,800 homes in 2026. The company said the revised outlook reflects slower sales activity as affordability pressures continue to weigh on demand.

The builder maintained the remainder of its full-year guidance, including an expected average sales price between $360,000 and $370,000 and adjusted home building gross margin between 22.5% and 24.5%.

“As we head into the final quarter of the year, our focus is on finishing 2026 strong,” Lipar said. “Affordability remains the key consideration for today’s buyers, and we have intentionally broadened our sales process to work with more prospective customers who may need additional time to qualify.”
