#5681. NYC Votes To Cut Construction Red Tape in Bid To Spur More Homebuilding

New York City voters overwhelmingly approved a plan to overhaul the city's notoriously complicated construction permitting process on Tuesday, handing Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory in his effort to accelerate housing development.

Question 4, 1 of 5 ballot measures approved in the Nov. 3 election, received roughly 68% support, according to preliminary election results.

The measure promises to simplify construction by bringing 40 types of permits and approvals currently handled by 18 separate government offices and agencies into one centralized digital system.

"New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do," Mamdani said in a statement on Tuesday night. The reforms would "directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love."

However, the new system isn't required to launch until 2030. Even when it does, faster permitting will address only one of the many obstacles making housing so difficult and expensive to build in New York.

"No single reform will be a silver bullet for housing supply and affordability, especially in a city like New York," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Instead, each pro-supply policy change is a baby step in the right direction. And these marginal gains will add up."

The Big Apple needs approximately 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to meet existing and future demand, according to an August 2026 draft assessment from the city's housing and planning departments.

Yet developers filed plans for just 8,064 multifamily units in the second quarter of 2026, in a stunning 52% decline from the previous quarter, according to the Real Estate Board of New York.

That amounts to less than half the 17,500 new homes the city needs to add each quarter—and they're only proposed units, not completed homes.

Centralizing permits could help close that gap by cutting down the time and cost builders are forced to spend navigating city bureaucracy.

"Streamlining approvals can make a huge difference," Krimmel says. "It might not be the flashiest reform, but when it comes to new construction, time is money."

And permitting takes a very, very long time in New York City.

Of the nearly five years it takes to build a typical 20-unit apartment building in the Big Apple, roughly 1.5 years are spent securing permits alone, according to a September 2026 study examining construction timelines across 60 U.S. cities.

Now compare that to similar projects in Raleigh, NC, or Phoenix, where it takes roughly two years from application to completion.

"In a city like New York City with high land acquisition costs and a complex regulatory environment, predictability in timelines and financing can be critical for ensuring new construction can pencil," Krimmel says.

Research suggests those time savings could translate into more homes.

Cutting approval times by 25% could have increased multifamily housing production in Los Angeles by 12.7% between 2010 and 2022, according to a 2026 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics.

When researchers accounted for additional development that faster approvals might encourage, the estimated increase reached 23.7%.

The question for New Yorkers, though, is when those reforms might translate into more housing options and lower rents. The median monthly asking rent hit $3,785 in October—up 4.5% from a year ago.

Under the new rules, applicants would have one digital portal to submit documents, track applications, and obtain approvals, rather than navigating separate systems across multiple agencies.

But streamlining applications doesn't necessarily mean they'll be reviewed any faster.

In fact, the average time required to approve applications through the Department of Buildings' existing digital portal climbed from 8.3 days in 2020 to 20.3 days in 2025, according to a July report from New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

And its hardly the only challenge. Krimmel says the overhaul won't address other barriers to construction, including zoning restrictions and the complexity of financing multifamily developments.

Still, he sees the reform as one step toward untangling a much larger problem.

"In the same way that a complex web of red tape and veto points is extremely good at creating barriers to new construction, real solutions will require the city untangles that web bit by bit," he says.

With the new system potentially four years away, the first test will be whether it actually shortens permitting timelines. Any corresponding increase in housing construction—and relief for renters—could take considerably longer.

As Mamdani acknowledged on Tuesday night, "Now comes the work of turning these votes into results."

#5680. These Markets Led New-Home Shopper Conversions in Q3

As housing affordability continues to challenge the market and overall shopper activity softens, understanding where prospective buyers are actively engaging becomes increasingly valuable for home building professionals.

Zonda’s latest Homebuyer Outlook shows Houston led major markets for new-home shopper conversions in Q3 2026. Atlanta ranked second, while Riverside rounded out the top three. Atlanta’s performance was particularly notable since the market came in seventh place in Q2 2026.

The results come from Zonda’s proprietary Conversion Index, which gives builders another way to assess buyer interest beyond traffic alone. The index measures the ratio of online shopper clicks to community tour requests on NewHomeSource.com, helping capture the point at which shoppers move beyond researching homes and toward engaging with a community.

While high levels of online shopping can indicate interest in a market, conversions show where consumers are taking a more meaningful action.

That distinction becomes especially useful in a slower demand environment. It also provides another perspective since online shopper activity softened but several markets recorded stronger conversion readings than in the previous quarter. That makes conversion a useful complement to traditional measures of demand.

#5679. North Carolina Passes New Limits on Property Tax Levies

On Tuesday, North Carolina voters narrowly approved House Bill 1089, which proposed a limit on property tax increases. The amendment needed 60% of voters to support it to pass. It received 60.4% support.

The amendment does not specify the terms of those limits. Instead, that will be up to the North Carolina General Assembly to decide.

Proponents, including North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, contended that surging property assessments have enabled local governments to impose excessive tax burdens on residents without delivering proportional public services.

Last year, Hall formed the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform, a 23-member committee to examine property taxes in the state.

“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in a press release earlier this year.

Support for the amendment fell across party lines. Conservatives and commercial organizations supported the measure, arguing that the amendment would help curb local government spending and protect property owners.

Political pundits theorized that the ballot measures were meant to entice Republican voters to the polls during an off-election year. But Western Carolina University professor Chris Cooper told NPR's All Things Considered the theory didn't hold much weight.

"The notion that North Carolinians were not going to show up and vote from the Republican persuasion, but now they are because of a constitutional amendment, is on there, frankly that stretches credibility for me a little bit."

But critics of the proposal said that creating a property tax cap would hobble local governments. Furthermore, the North Carolina Housing Coalition argued that the proposal would most benefit larger corporate property owners while providing little benefit to owners of single-family homes.

Tamika Walker Kelly, president of the North Carolina Association of Educators, criticized the bill for favoring “tax breaks over classrooms.”

“When local revenue is constrained, schools feel it immediately with overcrowded classrooms, aging school buildings, and educators stretched too thin,” Walker Kelly told NC Newsline. “A constitutional cap does not protect struggling families. It protects the largest landowners in the state, while the families who depend on public schools are left with less.”

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in North Carolina is 0.66%, which is relatively low compared with states such as New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

#5678. Smith Douglas Homes Grows Q3 Orders and Backlog as Margins Tighten

Smith Douglas Homes continued to grow orders and closings during the third quarter despite mounting affordability pressure. The challenging housing environment weighed heavily on the builder’s profitability.

The No. 33 builder closed 831 homes during the quarter, up 5% from 788 a year earlier. However, home closing revenue increased just 0.2% to $262.5 million as the average sales price of homes closed fell to approximately $316,000 from $333,000 in the prior-year period.

Net new home orders increased 13% to 777 from 690 a year earlier. The contract value of those orders rose to $246.1 million from $231.8 million, while the average sales price of orders declined to approximately $317,000 from $336,000. The quarterly cancellation rate was relatively stable at 11.3%, compared with 11.2% a year earlier.

Backlog increased 25% year over year to 947 homes at the end of September, with a contract value of $305.3 million.

“We continued to execute with discipline during the third quarter despite increasingly challenging housing market conditions,” said CEO and vice chairman Greg Bennett. “Higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures have weighed on buyer demand and profitability, but our teams remain focused on things we can control with respect to managing costs, building efficiently, and maintaining a steady absorption pace.”

While Smith Douglas Homes maintained its sales pace, profitability came under considerably more pressure. Home closing gross margin declined to 16.3% from 21% in the prior-year quarter. Pretax income fell to $3.3 million from $17.2 million, while diluted earnings per share declined to $0.07 from $0.24.

The builder’s lower average selling price highlights the affordability dynamic. The average price of homes closed decreased roughly 5% year over year to $316,000, while the average price of new orders declined about 6% to $317,000.

“While we expect market conditions to remain challenging in the near term, we remain confident in the long-term demand for affordable housing,” Bennett said. “Our priorities continue to be running an efficient home building operation and preserving our financial strength while remaining prepared to take advantage of opportunities as conditions improve.”

Smith Douglas Homes also continued expanding its community footprint during the quarter. The builder ended September with 113 active communities, up 15% from 98 a year earlier. Total controlled lots increased 2% to 24,724, including 22,693 optioned lots.

The company ended the quarter with 1,514 homes under construction, compared to 1,098 last year.

“Our disciplined approach to capital allocation and land investment remains particularly important in today’s operating environment,” said executive vice president and CFO Russ Devendorf. “Our land-light operating model, efficient construction cycle times, and conservative balance sheet provide us with the flexibility to manage through periods of weaker demand without compromising our long-term objectives.”

#5677. The chips are down: Qualcomm falls on revenue miss, weak guidance; Arm and GlobalFoundries do little better

Chipmakers Qualcomm Inc., Arm Holdings Ltd. and GlobalFoundries Ltd. struggled to move the needle today after reporting financial results that clearly left investors wanting more.

After an impressive earnings beat from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. just 24 hours earlier, investors may have had heightened expectations. But if they did, on a day when the market rocketed higher on the U.S. election results, they were clearly let down by the shaky performance of Qualcomm, which beat expectations on earnings but missed on revenue and offered weak guidance. The result was predictable, with its stock down more than 6% after-hours.

Both Arm and GlobalFoundries did better, but it wasn’t enough to satisfy investors who are becoming increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence industry that has driven significant growth for all three chipmakers over the last couple of years.

The biggest disappointment was Qualcomm, which reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8% from a year earlier. The results were mixed, with Wall Street looking for earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it’s looking for earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range on sales of $10.48 billion, falling short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share in earnings and $10.48 billion in revenue.

Qualcomm’s troubles stem from the fact that it has less exposure to the AI industry’s rampant growth than many other chipmakers. The bulk of its sales comes from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. But the market is currently reeling due to the rising cost of components such as memory, which have forced handset makers to bump up their prices, reducing demand. Qualcomm has tried to weather the storm by raising the prices of its own chips recently, but its smartphone chip sales fell 26% in the quarter to just $5.14 billion, well behind the Street’s target of $5.21 billion.

Under Chief Executive Cristiano Amon (pictured), Qualcomm has tried to pivot and grow its position in alternative chip markets, particularly the AI data center industry. Revenue from that segment rose to $650 million during the quarter, but it’s still dwarfed by the smartphone business.

Nonetheless, Amon insisted that the company will grow its data center business to more than $5 billion in revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. He said the company recently struck a deal with an unnamed global hyperscaler for optical connectivity chips. “We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” he told analysts on a conference call. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

Qualcomm’s automotive business was a bright spot, with sales there rising 89% to $1.99 billion in the quarter, above the Street’s consensus estimate of $1.66 billion. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4% from a year ago and just ahead of the Street’s estimate.

Finally, there’s Qualcomm’s QTL business, which generates revenue from licensing intellectual property for modems, 5G connectivity and other technologies. That segment added $1.3 billion in revenue, down 7%, despite signing renewed licensing agreements with Apple Inc., Transsion Inc. and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd.

Chip design company Arm delivered much more palatable results, but it was somewhat cautious with its guidance for the current quarter, and its stock was down 2% in late trading today. The company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27% from a year earlier, to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analyst estimate.

Unlike Qualcomm, Arm doesn’t manufacture complete chips for its customers, but instead designs and licenses processor blueprints for customers such as Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Qualcomm to build their own custom chips. Where Arm is more similar to Qualcomm is in its strategy, where it too is also pivoting to focus on data center chip designs, trying to tap into the demand for AI compute. Arm said its data center business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year-over-year.

However, Arm’s guidance did little to excite investors. The company said it’s looking for earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, compared with Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents per share. For revenue, it’s targeting $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, which is just ahead of the Street’s $1.52 billion target.

GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers today, posting results and guidance for the current that squeaked past expectations. However, its stock remained flat after-hours.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, with growth driven by strong demand from AI and data center customers, it said. The results were better than expected, with analysts targeting earnings of 51 cents on revenue of $1.89 billion.

GlobalFoundries’ also differs from Qualcomm, in that it’s a pure-play contract manufacturer that builds the processors designed by semiconductors firms, rather than designing chips itself or selling them under its own brand. Qualcomm is actually one of its biggest customers, alongside Broadcom Inc., NXP Semiconductors N.V. and Infineon Technologies Inc. As such, its fortunes are very much aligned with those of the chip designers it caters too.

For the current quarter, GlobalFoundries said it’s looking for earnings of 59 cents per share, plus or minus five cents, on revenue of about $2 billion. Wall Street is looking for earnings of 57 cents per share and has the same revenue target.

#5676. Why the Garage Could Be a Home’s Biggest Flood Weak Spot

When homeowners think about protecting their property from flooding, the garage may not be the first place that comes to mind. But with its wide entrance, ground-level access and potential gaps around the door, a garage can be a vulnerable point when floodwater collects around a home.

A garage door’s bottom seal can help keep out everyday rain, leaves and debris, but it should not be assumed to provide reliable protection against floodwater. During periods of heavy rainfall, water may collect on a driveway, pool against the garage entrance or find its way through gaps around the door and threshold.

And the damage may not stop at a wet garage floor. Floodwater can affect vehicles, tools, appliances and stored belongings, while water entering through a connecting doorway may also threaten the rest of the house.

Cui Guanhong, flood barrier product specialist at Eudore, explains why homeowners should pay closer attention to their garages when preparing for flooding.

“Homeowners should consider the garage as part of their overall flood-prevention plan, rather than focusing only on front doors and windows,” he says. “The condition of the garage door seal, the height of the threshold and the way water moves across the driveway can all affect how vulnerable the entrance may be.”

Unlike a standard exterior door, a garage door often spans a wide opening close to ground level. This creates a larger area where water may enter if the door does not close properly or the surrounding surfaces allow water to accumulate.

“It’s worth checking what happens around the garage entrance during heavy rain,” says Cui. “If water consistently pools near the door, that is a sign to investigate the drainage and the way the driveway directs water.”

The bigger worry is often what is already inside the garage, starting with anything plugged in.

“The electrical risk comes first,” says Cui. “Outlets, extension cords, a chest freezer or a charger left plugged in can all become dangerous if floodwater reaches them.”

Official flood safety guidance from Ready.gov advises against touching electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Never enter a flooded garage or stand in water to reach electrical equipment or a breaker.

Garages may also contain water heaters and other heating equipment that could be damaged if floodwater reaches them. The extent of the damage depends on the equipment, its location and the depth of the water. Additionally, items stored at floor level, including power tools, paint cans, and cleaning products may be damaged or contaminated if floodwater enters the garage.

The connecting door is the part Cui believes homeowners underestimate most.

“If a garage opens directly into a hallway, laundry room, mudroom or kitchen, water entering the garage could potentially spread into the home,” he says. “Homeowners should consider this connection when assessing their property’s flood risk.”

Floor drains are the last detail, and the one that trips people up. During severe flooding, water may back up through floor drains if the drainage system becomes overwhelmed.

“Whether a backwater valve makes sense depends on how the property’s drainage is laid out, so that is a question for a qualified plumbing professional rather than a guess,” says Cui.

The best time to check your garage’s flood vulnerabilities is before a flood warning is issued. Waiting until water is already collecting outside the door may leave little time to inspect the entrance, install a barrier or move vulnerable belongings. Homeowners can start by checking their property’s flood risk, monitoring local weather alerts and preparing a plan for moving vehicles and important items to safer locations when necessary.

FEMA’s flood maps resources can help homeowners find official flood hazard information for their area, although a map should not be treated as a guarantee that a property will or will not flood.

It is also worth reviewing insurance arrangements before an emergency. Most standard homeowners insurance policies do not cover flood damage, so homeowners should check their policy and explore separate flood insurance if appropriate. FloodSmart, run by the National Flood Insurance Program, provides further information about flood insurance coverage and options.

Five ways to reduce a garage’s flood risk

Inspect the garage door seal. Check the bottom seal for cracks, gaps or signs of wear. Close the garage door and look for visible openings along the bottom and sides. Replace damaged seals in line with the manufacturer’s instructions. A sound seal can help limit ordinary water and debris entering through gaps, but it should not be treated as a substitute for flood protection.

Check the driveway and drainage. Observe where rainwater flows during a storm. Does it collect near the garage door, or does the driveway direct it towards the entrance? Keep drains and channels clear of leaves and debris. If water repeatedly pools around the garage, consider asking a qualified drainage or building professional to assess the slope and drainage arrangements. Any changes should be designed so they do not redirect water onto neighboring properties.

Consider a suitable flood barrier. Where flooding is a concern, a purpose-designed garage flood barrier may offer an additional layer of protection. However, not every barrier is suitable for every opening or flood scenario. Before choosing a product, check the dimensions of the garage entrance, the condition and level of the surfaces where the barrier will sit, and the manufacturer’s installation instructions and performance limitations. A barrier may be less effective if it is incorrectly fitted or used outside its specified conditions. Homeowners should also understand how quickly the barrier can be installed and where it will be stored so it can be accessed when needed.

Protect equipment and stored belongings. Where practical, keep valuable tools, electronics and important belongings off the garage floor. Use suitable shelving or storage that reduces the chance of items being damaged by shallow water. Store paints, fuels, cleaning products and other hazardous materials securely and in accordance with their labels. If electrical equipment, heating systems or other utilities could be exposed to floodwater, seek professional advice on appropriate protective measures.

Look at the route from the garage into your home. If your garage connects directly to your house, consider whether water entering the garage could reach the connecting doorway or adjoining rooms. The layout and floor levels of each property are different, so homeowners should avoid assuming that a simple DIY alteration will solve the problem. If flooding has affected the property before, a qualified building or flood-mitigation professional may be able to identify vulnerable entry points and appropriate improvements.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5675. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

#5674. A $6.52 Million Beverlywood Home on a Lavish Golf Course Just Set the Record for the Priciest Teardown Sale

A Los Angeles property in Beverlywood has been sold in an off-market transaction, and at $6.52 million, it has set the record for the most expensive home to be purchased with plans to be torn down in the upscale neighborhood.

The dwelling is certainly in a coveted location, perched directly on the Hillcrest Country Club—a private club with an 18-hole golf course that has attracted celebrity members for more than a century.

According to Town and Country Magazine, the club’s initiation fee is a reported $185,000. Comedian Adam Sandler, singer-songwriter Neil Diamond, and Paramount co-founder Adolph Zukor are among the Hillcrest’s most notable members.

The home currently standing at 1807 Roxbury Drive is a three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom abode spanning 2,874 square feet. It was built in 1953.

According to Micah Hiller of Prime Rock Realty, who represented the seller and buyer of 1807 Roxbury Drive, the new residents are looking to build a new house with a luxury construction company called Drexel Luxury Homes. They’d like a home with a much larger footprint.

The lot itself is 8,660 square feet, and Hiller estimates the buyers will be able to build a home that’s “at least” 4,500 square feet without a basement. Should they decide to add a lower ground floor, they’d likely be able to add an additional 2,000 or 3,000 square feet.

“This is the highest land-value sale in Beverlywood’s history,” Hiller tells Realtor.com®.

Hiller explains that Beverlywood has become a highly sought-after enclave, which, “despite the current market, continues to show incredible strength.”

“From what I’m seeing, demand for the neighborhood has only grown, and in some ways, it has become even more desirable than Beverly Hills,” he continues. “Buyers appreciate the community, location, and opportunity to create a home here.”

Beverlywood has seen some year-over-year softness in the housing market with the median listing price, price per square foot, and median days on the market all showing decreases from this time last year, according to Realtor.com data.

Still, each of these metrics is outperforming nationwide stats. In Beverlywood, the average listing is just under $2.4 million, while that number is just under $420,000 for the country as a whole.

Homes here also spend less than half the time on the market than they do nationwide, with Beverlywood listings being snapped up in an average of 29 days. The U.S. median is 61.

For the Los Angeles neighborhood, this number is down 21.62% year over year, signaling faster turnover and a more competitive environment for sellers.

As of October 2026, Beverlywood had an impressive sale-to-list price ratio of 99%, indicating a strong seller’s market for this desirable spot. There are also fewer opportunities for a buyer to find exactly what they’re looking for, as there are only a dozen active listings for sale.

Beverlywood is not the only corner of the country with a competitive market setting records.

In Provincetown, MA—where the price per square foot is six times the national median—the record for most-expensive condo sold was broken twice in a two-week period.

Thomas Andrews of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, who was the listing agent on both pricey transactions, said the vibrant community is the reason the local market is so coveted—which is quite similar to what Hiller says of Beverlywood.

“Provincetown is such a magical place. You have your Martha’s Vineyard, you have your Nantucket, but there’s so much soul in the creative arts in Provincetown that just makes it super vibrant and super sought-after,” he said.

Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones explains that the town has effectively reached its limit for new housing, which creates a tense battle for anyone who wants to find a home there.

"Provincetown sits at the very tip of Cape Cod, which means there is essentially no more space to build," she explains. "The housing stock is therefore relatively fixed, and any new supply has to come off from redevelopment or small-scale infill, both of which tend to be expensive and difficult to pull off."

#5673. Homebuilder Stocks Surge as Democratic Sweep Raises Hopes for Affordability Gains

Homebuilders and housing suppliers saw significant jumps in their share prices following the stunning success of Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

At the closing bell on Wednesday, shares of major builders Lennar and PulteGroup were up more than 7% on the day, and D.R. Horton rose more than 8%.

Suppliers showed similar increases. Home Depot finished the day up 6.5%, after spiking as much as 17% during midday trading, according to Yahoo Finance. Lowe’s Companies ended the day up 7.5%, but also had a midday spike to 15% before giving back some gains.

For comparison, the broad S&P 500 index ended the day up 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%, or more than 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since April 2025.

The stock market surge comes in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm election, where Democrats gained control of Congress in a dramatic sweep.

The homebuilding sector has faced massive cost increases in recent years. Several factors have played into the building sector’s hardships, which have led to a shortfall of roughly 4 million homes throughout the U.S., according to a March report from Realtor.com®.

Tariffs, supply chain issues, and inflation have caused substantial increases in material costs, according to Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial Group.

“Labor continues to be a major issue, with a shortage of skilled workers driving wages higher,” Gestiehr tells Realtor.com. “Add in land prices, permitting, insurance, and financing costs, and it becomes increasingly difficult to build homes at prices the average buyer can afford.”

Builders have experienced a squeeze from both sides, Gestiehr explains, because at the same time that the cost to build a home has increased, skyrocketing mortgage rates have put limits on what buyers can afford.

Just days ago, major builders including D.R. Horton and the PulteGroup reported net income declines, with PulteGroup CEO Ryan Marshall stating that the company’s year-over-year net income dropped by 17% in the third quarter.

Suddenly, there’s a renewed sense of optimism surrounding the industry after Tuesday’s election results.

While the underlying challenges remain, Gestiehr says that investors are likely expecting more federal attention to turn to policies surrounding affordability.

“Housing affordability has become a major concern, and investors may be anticipating more attention on policies that encourage new construction and make homeownership more affordable,” says Gestiehr. “Investors may be anticipating additional housing incentives, policies that encourage new construction, and potentially lower mortgage rates.”

Affordability, particularly when it comes to housing, was a key part of many Democratic candidate platforms.

To address affordability overall, there should be focus on building up the supply of homes before offering incentives for buyers and spurring more demand, says Gestiehr.

"If you increase demand without increasing supply, you may end up pushing home prices even higher,” adds Gestiehr. “Reducing regulatory costs, streamlining permitting, encouraging additional development, and potentially lowering tariffs on building materials could all help builders.”

Rolling back tariffs was a major talking point for several incoming Democrat senators, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, as well as Alaska’s Mary Peltola, whose race results were pending.

Gestiehr maintains that many other factors, including inflation, interest rates, employment, and corporate earnings, as well as actual policy changes, will still have a much greater impact on homebuilder results than the election results alone. It’s not uncommon for markets to perform well following midterm elections, in part because the uncertainty surrounding the election is removed.

“The election may have given homebuilders a reason to be optimistic, but optimism doesn't necessarily translate into stronger earnings,” says Gestiehr. “At some point, these companies need to see improvement in demand, affordability, and profit margins to justify higher stock prices.”

Congress already passed one major bipartisan housing bill this year, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill lays out 45 provisions aimed at cutting red tape and constructing more homes, as well as banning institutional investor homebuyers.

Adding new members to Congress, many of whom have been elected on the promise of ushering in affordability, could mean more meaningful change is on the way.

“With a divided government, I wouldn’t expect major changes overnight, but housing affordability is an area where both parties have an incentive to find common ground,” says Gestiehr.

#5672. French blood banks hacked amid ‘deeply concerning’ wave of fridge and freezer cyberattacks in Europe

In a recent spate of cyberattacks in Europe against fridges and freezers, the latest assault hit France’s national blood service, where hackers gained control of cold storage systems at medical facilities and turned up the temperature.

The French Blood Establishment, EFS, told media that the facilities managed to save the blood supplies and there has been “no loss of blood products.” But the attacks come after supermarkets in several European countries experienced hacks of their fridges and freezers leading to the loss of millions of Euros in products.

Last month, hackers hit hundreds of supermarkets across France where temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees C overnight in what officials called an “unprecedented” attack. Food losses and fires were reported after “connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France.” What followed was a wave of similar attacks across the continent where fridges and freezers at stores in the U.K., Italy and Germany were recently hacked, following attacks in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” said EU Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

Connected fridges can now be controlled and monitored remotely through internet-connected software but with this comes vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit publicly reachable, legacy or unpatched remote refrigeration management controllers that may use default passwords or weak date-based administrative bypasses.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, told Reuters.

Cybersecurity experts so far have not figured out who’s behind the attacks. Russian hacking groups are a possibility as well as Iranian hacktivists or nation-state hackers. It might also be kids pulling off what have so far been very expensive pranks. Cybersecurity researchers at some firms have installed fake software as honeypots in an attempt to gather information about the hackers.

I took a lot of liberties in this apartment that I would not do in my family home or in my Greensboro home where I felt like it has to be more grown-up or something like that. I [felt] the freedom to be like, “That's the cutest thing I've ever seen. I'm gonna get that, whether it fits or not.”

#5668. Kyndryl shares surge 30% on hyperscaler-related revenue growth

Shares of Kyndryl Holdings Inc. jumped 30% today after it reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

Kyndryl generated $3.9 billion in sales during the three months ended Sept. 30. That represents a 1.9% decrease from a year earlier, but the company still managed to top the consensus estimate by about $50 million. It attributed the top-line surprise to its Kyndryl Consult business.

Kyndryl, a former IBM Corp. unit, once generated nearly all its revenue from managing other companies’ technology infrastructure. In 2022, it launched Kyndryl Consult to take on more strategic, higher-margin professional services deals.

The unit’s revenue grew 4.2% year-over-year in the second quarter. Kyndryl didn’t share a specific quarterly revenue number, but divulged that the unit earned a total of $3.6 billion over the past 12 months.

Kyndryl Consult’s signings, a measure of future revenue, jumped 19% over the past year. That momentum may have contributed to the company’s stock rally today.

Many of the projects that Kyndryl Consult takes on involve artificial intelligence. The unit can help customers build AI agent ensembles and set up training data generation pipelines. Additionally, it can advise clients about business decisions such as how they should allocate their AI budgets.

Kyndryl offers a software platform called Bridge to companies that buy its AI services. It enables AI agents to access business data from an organization’s internal systems. Additionally, Bridge monitors those agents to ensure they adhere to safety requirements.

The public cloud is another major focus of Kyndryl’s growth efforts. The company’s hyperscale-related revenue topped $500 million in the second quarter, which amounts to a 27% year-over-year increase.

“Strong signings and continued growth in Kyndryl Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue reinforce our confidence in our fiscal 2027 outlook,” said Kyndryl Chief Executive Officer Martin Schroeter. “Our performance reflects demand for Kyndryl’s AI-led modernization capabilities and deep mission-critical expertise that help customers evolve their complex technology environments, strengthen cybersecurity and achieve measurable business outcomes.”

The company delivered an adjusted net income of $92 million, which breaks down to 42 cents per share. Analysts expected 41 cents per share. The sum excludes a $38 million workforce reduction charge the company took in the second quarter. It’s part of a broader cost-cutting initiative that is set to save up to $500 million annually starting from Kyndryl’s 2028 fiscal year.

For the current fiscal year, the company is forecasting an adjusted pretax income of $600 million to $700 million. Kyndryl expects its revenue to be flat or increase by up to 2%.

#5667. Real REMAX Q3 Revenue Skyrockets; Company ‘Offboards’ Over 1,000 Agents

After the Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of RE/MAX Holdings this past August, the third quarter earnings for the company revealed a significant shift in revenue, sparked by AI investments and slight drops in agent retention.

Tamir Poleg—Real REMAX chairman and CEO—started off the first earnings call for the combined companies, and expressed his confidence in “delivering strong growth in adjusted EBITDA” even if the housing market “gets worse.”

He also acknowledged the increases in agent offboarding. The Q3 earnings release stated that 500 agents had been let go in October alone, with the total REMAX agent count in the U.S. and Canada reportedly down 3% from the previous year at 72,118.

“The housing market has been operating near trough levels for the past four years,” Poleg added. “The recent increase in mortgage rates has further delayed the recovery that many, myself included, had anticipated. Beginning in September, we saw an uptick in the number of agents leaving the industry altogether. Real REMAX Group was not immune. Over the past two months, we’ve proactively offboarded more than 1,000 agents, many of whom allowed their real estate licenses to expire or left the industry.”

Real REMAX Group President Jenna Rozenblat echoed Poleg’s sentiment and noted that personnel other than agents were let go throughout the third quarter.

“We’ve reduced our combined headcount by more than 14%, which translates to over 150 positions across the organization while simplifying management structures and consolidating overlapping functions,” she stated.

While the series of layoffs and offboarding can be a cause for concern for some agents, Rozenblat emphasized the reason why restructuring is taking place, and mentioned the importance of AI technology.

“We don’t expect an immediate reversal in agent attrition in a franchise business, but our priority is to improve franchise owner economics and help them deliver a more competitive value proposition to agents and the clients they serve,” she continued. “Technology is an important part of that effort. We have already begun alpha testing Real’s proprietary reason software and AI capabilities for a phase rollout to the broader REMAX network.”

Poleg also briefly addressed a question on Open Real Estate, the initiative promising a new platform for listing distribution.

Poleg said Real REMAX believed strongly in its principles of “a more open, transparent and competitive approach to how real estate data is distributed,” but declined to comment on “specific products, economics or revenue opportunities” stemming from Open Real Estate.

On the point of AI, October’s introduction of Leo Pro—Real REMAX’s AI platform for agents and brokerages—could have instigated the large offboarding process. Poleg pointed out how Leo Pro can perform the functions “that traditionally required hiring additional staff, paying for multiple software subscriptions or spending hundreds of hours doing the work yourself.”

“The main usage of Leo Pro we’re seeing is creating marketing materials, social media posts and working their CRMs. It’s mostly nurturing their leads, and we’re seeing great conversions for our agents in terms of scheduling appointments for them and listing agreements,” Poleg stated.

Poleg also claimed that “historically, there has been a lot of disappointment with what REMAX has been offering their agents and brokers” in terms of tech, and that he has seen a lot of excitement from franchise owners.

“The fact that we have mature technology that is serving the Real side on the brokerage side gives them a lot of confidence that this is proven technology that can help them run better businesses,” Poleg said.

The data for the Q3 earnings call predates the release of Leo Pro.

Overall, the Real REMAX Group’s revenue increased 28% on a yearly basis, clocking in at nearly $728 million for Q3. The Q3 revenue for 2025 was $568.5 million.

The jump in revenue can mostly be attributed to the acquisition, as the release also notes that assuming the acquisition had taken place on Jan. 1, 2025 (a pro forma basis). It’s estimated that the combined revenue had increased by 20% instead to $770 million, compared to the prior year’s $641.8 million.

“On a pro forma basis, combined revenue increased 20% year-over-year to approximately $770 million compared with a 2% decline in industry existing-home sales transactions in the quarter,” Real REMAX CFO Ravi Jani said. “Within our brokerage business, Real continued to gain market share, while our franchise business continues to see attrition in North America.”

As for profitability, the company’s operating loss clocked in at $72 million for the third quarter, a significant increase from last year’s loss of $0.5 million. Jani attributed the growth in operating loss to the $52.3 million in acquisition-related expenses, and another $26.4 million in accelerated stock-based compensation related to employee terminations following the acquisition.

Net loss also grew dramatically year-over-year, at $67.2 million—or $2.25 per diluted share—for Q3. Last year’s Q3 net losses were estimated to be $0.3 million, or only $0.02 per diluted share.

Despite significant growth in losses and expenses—primarily caused by the acquisition—Real REMAX’s adjusted EBITDA increased 66% to $33.8 million in Q3, compared to $20.4 million the same period last year. The adjusted EBITDA margin also increased slightly by 4.6%, whereas last year’s margin was 3.6%.

For the final quarter of 2026, Jani expects revenue to fall, while EBITDA maintains itself in the mid-$30 million range.

“For the fourth quarter of 2026, we’re expecting continued pressure on housing activity, including declines in transactions per agent at Real and a year-over-year decline in REMAX’s North American agent count,” he concluded. “Against that backdrop, we expect fourth quarter revenue of $575 million to $625 million and adjusted EBITDA of $32 million to $38 million.”

Leo Pro may take center stage in the company’s Q4 earnings call and throughout 2027, as Poleg mentioned that plans to roll out the AI platform for the entire REMAX network are underway.

“Within a few weeks, we want to roll out Leo Pro for the entire REMAX network. Our operating platform for the broker/owners will be ready at some point in Q1 2027,” Poleg added. “I think that once that’s in place, we will be able to help a lot of the broker/owners with some of their struggles around profitability, freeing up time to focus on agent attraction and teaching their agents on how to sell more.”

#5666. Generational Wealth Fuels Record-High Levels of Cash Sales Among First-Time Buyers

The share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash has climbed to record levels, fueled by generational wealth transfers, even as eroding affordability continues to push homeownership out of reach for many Americans.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 10% of rookie home shoppers paid all cash instead of relying on financing, marking the largest percentage on record, according to the annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors®.

The data also reveals that all-cash buyers were roughly three times likelier than financed first-time buyers to have used an inheritance (28% vs. 9%).

Across all first-time buyers—cash or financed—10% used an inheritance toward their home purchase, marking a new record and the fourth straight annual increase.

"The housing market is beginning to see a generational transfer of wealth. It’s not yet a tsunami, but it is changing who can buy a first home and when," says Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Because people are living longer, the generation receiving that wealth isno longer young adults. Many are reaching middle age before they can buy their first home."

In fact, while the median age of first-time buyers held steady at a record high of 40, cash buyers skewed older, with the median age reaching 54 years old, compared to 38 for those who used financing.

Echoing Lautz, Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones confirms that the transfer of wealth from one generation to the next is starting to show up in the housing market, though the full effect won't likely be felt for a few more years.

Older homeowners hold substantial equity, and repeat buyers, with a median age of 62—matching a record high set last year— paid all cash 30% of the time in 2026. Jones says that for some rookie buyers, that wealth arrives as an inheritance.

"Buyers with access to inherited wealth have a significant advantage when they can purchase without financing," Anthony Mian, an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills, tells Realtor.com. "In multiple-offer situations, sellers often favor all-cash offers because they eliminate financing risk, reduce the likelihood of delays, and provide greater certainty of closing."

Other avenues open to baby boomers wishing to boost their children's or grandchildren's purchasing power include cash gifted toward a down payment, co-signing a loan, or selling investment properties, says Emilee Warner, a real estate agent at MW Real Estate Co. in Nashville, TN.

Looking at the top sources for a down payment among first-time buyers, personal savings continued to dominate (62%), followed by financial assets, such as 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency (30%), and gifts or loans from family and friends (25%).

"Wealth, whether built up or inherited, is increasingly what gets some buyers in, while buyers who depend on a mortgage still face high rates and prices," notes Jones.

Warner says she recently worked with first-time buyers who paid all cash borrowed the "bank" of mom and dad to purchase a home with a price tag exceeding $1 million.

"The cash buyers out there want to get in a home prior to rates dropping," Warner tells Realtor.com. "They are serious, willing, and able buyers. Cash allows appraisals to be waived, removing the risk of a low appraisal that could lose a financed buyer the home."

While more than half of repeat buyers (57%) relied on proceeds from the sale of their previous home and 42% used savings for their down payment, harnessing generational wealth among this cohort is not unheard of, with 4% using an inheritance or a gift from a family member or friend to fund their next home purchase.

Brandon Winn, an agent at Iowa Realty in Des Moines, IA, says he recently worked with move-up buyers who were purchasing a home with the help of their parents who offered them a 3% loan.

"This was when interest rates were 6.5%, and they gave them a 3% loan so they could afford to buy the home that they wanted," Winn tells Realtor.com.

Winn adds that at the luxury tier of the Des Moines market topping $600,000, he is seeing a growing number of buyers paying all cash using either inheritance or investment funds.

"Interest rates have risen so quickly that it's priced a lot of buyers out of the market," says the agent. "So if you have the cash ... it gives you the opportunity to purchase the house without having a [mortgage] payment, and then, of course, you're going to build equity quite a bit faster."

Mian, in Beverly Hills, says that for young families, that additional disposable income can go toward childcare, education, savings, or investments. Access to generational wealth can even expand their housing search geographically.

"In a market as expensive as Los Angeles, this can influence not only who can afford to purchase a home, but also which neighborhoods they can access and how much financial flexibility they retain after purchasing," he says. "Ultimately, generational wealth is becoming an important factor in determining both housing opportunities and long-term financial security."

Affordability continues to be the biggest major hurdle for aspiring U.S. homeowners.

The share of first-time buyers ticked up to 22% from last year's all-time low of 21%, yet it is still roughly half the historical norm of 40% recorded before 2008. Jones attributes the modest year-over-year boost to mortgage rate declines in the beginning of 2026.

Rates briefly dipped below 6% in February, before the outbreak of the Iran war, and were below year-ago levels from October 2025 through July 2026.

"This presented a window of opportunity for first-time buyers relying on a mortgage. The vast majority of first-time buyers financed their purchase, which means the median first-time buyer age is closer to the financed first-time buyer age," says Jones. "All-cash first-time buyers have aged 10 years in a decade, versus six for financed buyers, which shows they are a different group, middle-aged and drawing on savings, investments or inheritance."

Examining the makeup of first-time buyers in 2026, NAR data shows the share of first-time buyers who were married couples decreased slightly to 47%. Single women accounted for a quarter of all first-time buyers, same as in 2025, while the share of single men climbed to 12%, the highest level since 2011.

The typical novice buyer in 2026 had a median household income of $100,000, up from last year's $94,400.

The median down payment among first-time buyers this year was 9%, down from 10% in 2025 and significantly below the 18% recorded among all buyers.

As in years past, equity-rich repeat buyers continued to dominate the market, accounting for 78% of all home purchases with a median household income of $127,000 and a typical down payment of 19%— more than double that of first-timers. Nearly a third (30%) paid all cash.

"Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," says Lautz. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity."

The typical home seller in 2026 has owned their property for 12 years, a new all-time high surpassing last year's 11-year tenure. Forty-seven percent of sellers went on to purchase a newer home, and 36% bought a larger home.

Of all homes sold on the market, 78% did not have children under the age of 18 residing in the home, down from 81% last year.

For all sellers, the most commonly cited reason for selling their home was the desire to move closer to friends and family (22%), followed by the home being too small (12%), the home being too large (10%), a change in family situation (8%), and moving due to retirement (8%).

For recently sold homes, the final sales price was a median of 99% of the final listing price.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5665. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5664. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

#5663. Inside Cristiano Ronaldo’s Jaw-Dropping Global Property Portfolio and $1.4 Billion Fortune—as He Retires From International Football

Soccer legend Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international football after representing Portugal for 23 years.

"A journey that began in August 2004 and changed my life forever is coming to an end," the soccer icon said in a Nov. 5 Instagram post. "When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer."

For now, Ronaldo will continue to play at the club level with Al-Nassr FC in the Saudi Pro League. His contract extends through June 30, 2027.

The announcement comes months after the whistle was blown on his final World Cup in July. The former Portuguese captain and his team missed out on a spot in the 2026 quarterfinals with a devastating 0-1 loss to Spain in Texas.

Following an incredibly tense and largely goal-less matchup between the two teams, Spain's Mikel Merino managed to slide one past the Portuguese goalie in the 91st minute, cementing his team's place in the quarterfinal game.

Ronaldo, 41, was incredibly emotional as he walked off the pitch—hours after confirming at a press conference that the 2026 FIFA World Cup would be the last he plays in.

Ronaldo—whose country is set to co-host the World Cup in 2030 alongside Spain and Morocco—made the announcement during a July 5 press conference, just one day before Portugal's highly anticipated Round of 16 showdown against Spain in Dallas.

"It's about enjoying it as much as possible. This will be my last World Cup, but let's hope tomorrow isn't my last game," the star athlete said, according to ESPN.

The soccer icon noted that he has a "passion" for football, teasing that he hasn't done "too badly" on the field.

"I don't need it, I have a good life, but it's about passion. I play football because I love it. ... You have to enjoy every day. And I've scored three goals [at this World Cup], I'm not doing too badly, right?" Ronaldo said.

During the 2026 World Cup, Ronaldo became the first player to score in six World Cups when he achieved two goals against Uzbekistan.

Ronaldo marked another career highlight when he scored a penalty against Croatia in the Round of 32, which recorded his first goal in a knockout-round match of a World Cup.

Speaking about this year's tournament, the soccer legend noted, "It's been fantastic. It goes beyond the pitch. ... This is the World Cup I'll remember the most, because of people's passion. It's even more this time, I don't know why. It's been, emotionally, the best. I've enjoyed it very much."

"I'm not lacking anything in life. I'm not going to be more, or less, Cristiano because I win the World Cup. We have the qualities to win, but only one country can win it. ... Age gives you maturity and experience," he said.

Ronaldo has showcased his skills in six World Cup tournaments: 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026.

He said that he is grateful for the ups and downs he has experienced throughout that 20-year run, noting that he is even happy to have received public criticism because it has helped him to become a better player.

"I'm thankful even for the attacks I receive, turning 40—and I hope to live another 40 years—with the criticism. That's how you grow the most as a person, and I thank you, journalists, for that," Ronaldo said.

Off the field, Ronaldo has recently entered a new chapter. In August, he married his longtime partner, Georgina Rodriguez in a "private and intimate" ceremony in Portugal. He had proposed in 2025 after eight years of dating.

Ronaldo, who was born and raised in Portugal, began his professional playing career at age 17, when he made his debut for local team Sporting CP. He then moved to the U.K., where he joined Premier League team Manchester United.

During his 23-year career, Ronaldo has become one of the highest-paid soccer players in history, amassing a net worth of $1.4 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. He was, as a result, the first soccer star to become a verified billionaire.

In addition to his very lucrative contracts with some of the world's most elite soccer teams, the player has made an impressive amount of money through endorsement deals representing high-profile brands, including Armani, Nike, and TAG Heuer.

He has also amassed an incredibly impressive property portfolio throughout his career, snapping up homes in his native Portugal, as well as several dwellings farther afield.

Now, as the five-time Ballon d'Or winner calls time on his final FIFA World Cup, attention is once again turning to the legacy he will leave behind—not only through his record-breaking career, but also through an enviable collection of multimillion-dollar homes stretching from Portugal to Saudi Arabia.

Ronaldo first picked up a property in Portugal's capital in 2015 for $2 million.

The dwelling is located on Avenida da Liberdade, a boulevard that is inspired by Paris' Champs-Elysees and is adorned with boutiques, hotels, and cafes.

In 2018, he purchased a 3,100-square-foot-penthouse for $7 million, making history with the then-most expensive apartment ever sold in the city.

The property boasts three bedrooms, wood floors, a terrace, and glass walls that allow natural light to flood inside.

The home also features a spa, gym, and resort-style pool.

From 2009 to 2018, Ronaldo played for Real Madrid and sealed his legacy when he became the club's all-time leading scorer.

In 2010, the soccer star snapped up a luxe mansion in the La Finca neighborhood, a gated community known for its celebrity residents and 24/7 security.

The property, which was designed by Joaquín Torres, sprawls across 8,600 square feet.

It comes complete with a spa, cyrochamber, indoor pool, and even a soccer field.

In 2023, he placed the property on the market for rent for about $11,000 a month.

Ronaldo also made sure to pick up a property where he grew up—in Madeira, Portugal.

He splashed out $8 million for the seven-story abode, which was transformed from a former nightclub in 2015.

The dwelling boasts a rooftop pool, two gyms, and an indoor pool.

Although Ronaldo isn't always able to make it there, his mother and brother reportedly reside there full time.

By 2018, the soccer star picked up another pad in one of Turin's most lavish communities: Strada San Vito Revigliasco.

Inside, the home boasts chic marble, a spa, a gym and several resort-style pools.

After picking up a property in Turin, Ronaldo took a vacation to Marbella, Spain, and decided that he needed a getaway in the area.

The $1.6 million dwelling is situated in the development known as "Superstars' Cul-de-Sac."

The area is famous for its celebrity residents, including Conor McGregor, and offers panoramic views of the Mediterranean and several golfing areas.

His holiday home features four bedrooms, high ceilings, glass walls, a pool, a gym, a wine cellar, and a lavish home theater.

Elsewhere in Portugal, Ronaldo purchased a 2.47-acre plot built in the lavish Quinta da Marinh for $30 million.

The sprawling property was built between 2022 and 2023.

It comes complete with a home theater, spa, tennis court, two pools, and 30-car garage.

In 2022, the pro athlete moved to Riyadh to join Saudi Arabian team Al-Nassr—initially relocating to the Kingdom Centre Hotel, where he and his family lived for an entire month before settling down at a full-time residence.

That property is located in Al-Muhammadiyah, one of Riyadh’s most exclusive enclaves.

His home reportedly boasts modern lighting, a three-car garage, a lavish pool, and a luxe walk-in closet.

In 2024, Ronaldo picked up a home in Dubai's Jumeirah Bay Island, also known as "Billionaires Island."

The waterfront mansion is situated in a man-made enclave that can be accessed only by a private bridge.
