#5597. Los Angeles votes all-in on housing, electing YIMBY-backed Raman

Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles as YIMBY groups framed the race around accelerating housing production. City timelines for statewide SB 79 transit oriented housing rules, currently delayed to 2030, are expected to face pressure under the new administration.  AI Summary

City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass to become the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, a win for the “yes in my backyard” groups that backed her challenge to the incumbent.

The Associated Press called the race Thursday. Raman, an urban planner and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, led by 4.2 percentage points, 52.1% to 47.9%, with roughly 76% of the expected vote counted.

She is the second DSA member to lead a major U.S. city. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani won a year ago on an affordability platform that made more housing a focal point. Bass conceded and promised a “smooth and seamless transition.” She is the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a reelection bid.

Raman won despite long odds. Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, retiring former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and nearly every City Council member backed Bass.

YIMBY Action, YIMBY Los Angeles and California YIMBY were among the housing groups behind Raman. Unions, progressive Democratic organizations, environmental groups and County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath also endorsed her.

Housing and homelessness drove the campaign. Raman pitched expanded medical teams for people in encampments and moving residents out of city-rented hotels into permanent housing. She said she could cut encampments by at least half by 2028.

YIMBY groups cast the race as a test of how fast the city builds. The movement pushes to ease zoning limits and speed approvals to expand supply.

“Her win in California’s largest city is a big moment for the pro-housing movement,” California YIMBY posted on social media.

One early test is how Los Angeles complies with Senate Bill 79, the state law that encourages more housing near transit. City ordinances that took effect June 30 hold off full compliance citywide until 2030. YIMBY advocates will likely press the new mayor and council to move that date up. Raman favored a quicker housing timeline.

Mayor-elect Raman could inherit a $20 million-plus liability if the city doesn’t approve Woodland Hills Country Club’s 398-home plan. The club’s attorney, Dave Rand, a Raman supporter, set a 60-day deadline, and the state housing department wants a response by Nov. 25.

Raman will need the council to do that. Most members backed Bass, so Raman must build a majority from a body that largely opposed her.

She will have allies elsewhere at City Hall. Controller Kenneth Mejia and newly elected City Attorney Marissa Roy, a DSA member, join her in what The Hollywood Reporter called a “triumvirate of progressivism” at the top of city government.

#5596. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

To hear the full conversation with Ronen Schwartz, check out the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast. To learn more about how Google Cloud Storage can support the evolving demands of enterprise AI, explore Google’s storage solutions or connect with the Google Cloud team to discuss the right approach for your organization’s workloads.

#5595. Compass boosts exclusive listings while weighing Open Real Estate

Compass CEO Robert Reffkin praised the Open Real Estate initiative and said the company might participate. He emphasized Compass private exclusive inventory, 89,000 early listings on Compass.com and rising traffic, while the firm posted Q3 pro forma revenue of $3.90 billion and net income of $63 million.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin is not ruling out the possibility that his firm joins national residential real estate data-sharing initiative Open Real Estate.

“We welcome this change. It actually validates what we’ve been saying for the better part of two years, and so we are really excited to see the four of them lead in this way and to see others join,” Reffkin said during his firm’s third quarter 2206 earnings call with investors and analysts Thursday evening.

“In terms of joining or not, I think there’s definitely a path, but Compass International Holdings is definitely excited that there will be a national real estate listing service that will return the power back to the creator of the listing, the homeowner and their trusted agent, and that it’s good news for all agents and for all their clients, and we’re looking forward to seeing if there’s a way for us to be involved.”

Despite his praise for the initiative, which was founded by four of his largest competitors in the brokerage space and aims for fair and equal access to listing data, Reffkin also noted the growth of his firm’s private exclusive inventory.

As of early November, Reffkin said Compass had 89,000 listings on its site users could see on Compass.com prior to them being available to view on public listing portals. Additionally, Reffkin noted that in cities where there are no restrictions on the public marketing of office exclusive listings, on average this week, 63% of newly launched listings in the Compass brand employ its three-phase marketing strategy.

“We also hit over 70% adoption in some of these cities during the quarter, suggesting that as the industry’s artificial restrictions on homeowners and seller choice are removed, the good majority of listings would start off as a private exclusive or coming soon, and be a See It First listing on Compass.com and our sister company sites,” Reffkin said.

During the quarter, the company noted that traffic to its apps and websites was up 53.6% annually, according to data from SimilarWeb, and in September alone, after the launch of Compass’s new See It First offering halfway through the month, traffic was up 68% year over year.

“I would expect traffic to continue to increase as we’ve launched the See It First campaign,” Reffkin said. “The See It First campaign is also part of a rebranding exercise. I think some of our competitors have tried to brand the listings that we have as hidden but clearly, all of our listings are available to all agents and to all buyers. And when you call them ‘See It First,’ then it’s pretty clear we just want you to see it first on our site.”

In addition, building Compass.com’s inventory of listings comes with some added benefits in the AI-age. According to Reffkin, if you set up a search in a large language model (LLM) and ask it to alert you to any new listings in a given geography, “more often than not” it is providing consumers with Compass International Holdings listings.

“It is the new search alert, For anyone that wonders how are you going to find all the listings, if they’re not all in one site, well, Instinct and Muse prove that it’s just a different search alert. And it brings you to wherever the data comes first and whoever is the original author of the listing, which is obviously the listing agent, not a portal. And then they’re bringing you to listings that have more information,” Reffkin said.

This internal private listing network is also integrated into Compass’s Home platform, which the company is still in the process of rolling out to owned-brokerage agents. Company executives said that as of the end of October, they had successfully onboarded 33,950 agents. They expect to onboard the remainder of the 46,000 owned-brokerage agents by the end of 2026. Additionally, they said that they are on track to roll out the platform to all real estate professionals in their franchise network starting in Q1 2027.

By increasing the number of agents utilizing the platform, Reffkin said they are able to exponentially increase the number of client contacts within Compass’s database.

“We have 225 million unique contacts, and when you give me your listing, boom! It instantly pops up in their saved searches and I could then bring these buyers to your home,” Reffkin said.

Reffkin recounted the story of a Compass agent in Houston who had a client that wanted to relocate to Dallas. With Dallas being in a different MLS, the agent was unable to see MLS listings there, but within the Home platform, the agent could see all Compass International Holdings private exclusives in the city. According to Reffkin, the agent sent these listings to their client and the client ended up purchasing one that was listed by a Sotheby’s International Realty agent.

“That is a transaction that is across geographies and that would not be possible without the home platform,” Reffkin said. “That’s the power of the platform, where it is no longer restricting how people work, but creating much more flexibility and opportunity for the clients of our agents.”

In the third quarter, Compass International Holdings recorded an 11.6% annual increase in revenue on a pro forma basis, which assumes it had closed its acquisition of Anywhere on Jan. 1, 2025, to $3.90 billion. The firm’s net income came in at $63 million, up from a $4 million net loss a year ago. This marked the company’s first profitable third quarter. In addition, executives noted the company recorded a 6% annual decline in operating expenses on a pro forma basis.

“This was driven by the strong financial discipline that we’ve instilled into the organization over the past four years, and an acceleration of some cost synergy actions in light of the current environment. As of last week, we have actioned $360 million in net cost synergies compared to the $330 million full-year target for 2026,” Reffkin said. “We shared last quarter, and we remain fully committed to our $500 million-dollar target in less than three years.”

Reffkin also noted that the company is laser focused on agent attraction, retention and growth. The firm’s owned-brokerage operation closed the quarter with 85,476 agents, an increase of more than 2,000 agents from a quarter prior. This came as the firm lost 4,098 agents over the course of the quarter. But Compass noted that 58% of these separations reflected agents with $0 gross commission income (GCI) in the past 12 months — and 74% of separations reflected agents with $20,000 or less in GCI.

Owned-brokerage agents closed 140,118 transactions during the quarter with a gross transaction value of $138.9 billion. Franchise agents closed 191,809 transactions, totaling $108.9 billion in value.

Reffkin the firm expects to see further growth in agent count and productivity.

“The number of opportunities added to our growth team’s weekly active pipeline is up 39% quarter to date, compared to the second and third quarter of this year. Our walkover pipeline is also sitting at the highest levels we’ve seen year to date,” Reffkin said. “We believe the stronger recruiting pipeline we are seeing today is being driven by a flight to quality, as agents seek out brokerages that can provide them with technology and tools to help grow their business in a challenging market.”

Executives also touched upon the recent merger of mortgage joint ventures Guaranteed Rate Affinity and OriginPoint, which created a top-10 mortgage lender. The combined JV will operate under the OriginPoint brand moving forward.

During the third quarter, the total funded loan volume across OriginPoint and Guaranteed Rate Affinity was $3.30 billion, up 9.9% year over year on a pro forma basis.

Executives said a perk of now being a top-10 lender is that they have seen an uptick in interest from loan officers wanting to join the operation. Looking ahead, Reffkin said they want to be a top-5 retail lender.

“We’re obviously very committed to the business. We’re committed to ensuring that our real estate professionals and their clients are able to have everything in one place, which is not just technology, not just marketing, not just branding, but for title, escrow and mortgage as well,” Reffkin said.

#5594. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5591. Numbers tell a story. Are you uncovering the right ones?

Surface conversion rates can mislead sales managers when lead mix skews to harder credit buckets. Reviewing credit-bucket conversion and PQ-to-lock rates can pinpoint coaching opportunities and process leaks.   AI Summary

Helping loan originators get clarity on their business is important, especially when the headwinds can easily cause us to lose focus. How can we help our loan originators get more out of what they already have?

While analyzing some data recently, I dug for clarity I could share with a few LOs to help them better leverage what was already working at the top of the funnel.

The first case study was a branch that, on paper, showed a conversion problem. You know the story. How many of our at-bats are making it to the closing table? When I examined this branch, I found they were converting far below the company average.

Easy one. I can simply have a conversation with them about conversion and coach them through some strategies to help them convert better. Let’s take a deeper dive, though, and look at conversion based on credit buckets.

Looking at five different credit buckets, the story started to change. Yes, conversion was still weaker, but the reason why started to become clear.

The at-bats this branch was getting were coming from credit buckets that are harder to convert. Comparing the credit buckets, we found that they were converting higher-credit-score borrowers at the same pace as the rest of the company. Lower-credit-score borrowers and borrowers without a qualifying credit score were a large part of their top of funnel.

This was the reason their conversion was off.

Had I not dug deeper, a coaching conversation could have gone wrong, and we could have focused on some of the wrong things.  The layers of data are important, and we shouldn’t look at just what the surface tells us.

That led me even deeper, where I started to analyze credit-bucket conversion to see what was being left on the table. Yes, there were MLOs who had left significant dollars on the table because they weren’t converting the best borrowers at the same pace as the company average. This coaching conversation becomes about showing up as a vendor or as an advisor.

After all, a high-credit-score borrower knows who they are, and they also know they can get a loan anywhere. If you are just going to point them to a URL, you are teaching them they can get the same level of service and expertise at any URL.

If you’re a data nerd like me, you’ve stuck around to see what’s next.

One of the harder conversations in our business is giving clarity to a top producer about possible leaks in their business. After all, they are in the top 1% in the country among all originators, perennial President’s Club winners and have 5-star reviews in the thousands on lock.

Now imagine that top producer having an absolute banger of a year. Year-over-year volume and units are crushing the year before. The top-line numbers are fun. It’s sexy. It’s what everyone is looking at. Sometimes, though, it doesn’t hurt to take a bit of a deeper look.

In this case, you wouldn’t be surprised to find that this producer is also getting way more at-bats at the top of the funnel than they did the year prior.

If numbers tell a story and the numbers help us get clarity, where else should we look? In this case, I looked at conversion.

PQ-to-funding conversion is important. I looked at a different number, and that was PQ-to-lock conversion. It’s an earlier indicator than PQ-to-funding, and when the closings are coming in much hotter than a year before, you would think those numbers would be moving in parallel all the way through.

What we uncovered was that, compared with the same period the year before, lock conversion was down. Sometimes one of the byproducts of success is that we don’t see the whole field.

Think back to 2020 and 2021. When business was coming at us that fast, it was easy for inefficiencies to hide underneath production. Even today, when winning at a high level, it’s easy to overlook the tiny leaks.

The numbers underneath production told us there was still an opportunity to improve even more. The hard work of creating additional opportunities was already being done. A few adjustments in how those opportunities were handled could create an even greater increase in closed business.

Bryan Lovell is Vice President of Sales at Highland Mortgage.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5589. Here’s how the midterms could reset Washington’s housing agenda

Housing affordability is expected to be a top issue for the next Congress. Lawmakers may pursue a ROAD 2.0 package and funding for ROAD programs, while clashing with the Trump administration on tariffs, immigration, and affordable housing spending.  AI Summary

The rising cost of living was a catalyst that drove voters to the polls this week, so housing, which makes up a substantial share of that burden, could gain traction as a top priority once again for the incoming Congress.

Lawmakers in both parties want to address the high cost of housing. The question always is how much they can accomplish. Democrats, who will control the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives, may seek common ground with the Trump administration on housing policy, including streamlining regulations and funding the new programs created under the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

However, they could also clash with the administration over hot-button policy debates such as tariffs on building materials, immigration enforcement on construction sites and funding for affordable housing programs, among other issues.

Despite potential areas of agreement and disagreement, Andy Winkler, managing director of housing and infrastructure policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, said voters’ focus on affordability should keep housing high on the federal policy agenda.

“Housing costs, just like other rising costs of living, were clearly top of mind as voters headed to the polls. So, it appears to me that housing would continue to be a priority in the next Congress because of that,” Winkler said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Many housing advocates have pointed to the possibility of a “ROAD 2.0” bill as a follow-up to the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which became law on July 11 after securing overwhelming bipartisan support, with 85 votes in the Senate and 358 votes in the House of Representatives.

Winkler sees significant potential for another bipartisan housing package, despite potential divisions between Congress and the Trump administration. While the original legislation drew on about 60 different bills, many other bipartisan proposals failed to make the final package and could be revisited in the next Congress.

In October, the bipartisan Build America Caucus released a document previewing policy priorities that could shape a second housing bill. The bipartisan agenda included housing proposals aimed at expanding where homes can be built, lowering construction costs and improving access to financing.

The document’s focus points include establishing federally incentivized “Right to Build Zones” with by-right approvals, encouraging housing near transit, opening underused federal properties to residential development, modernizing fragmented building codes, and establishing a federal revolving loan fund for housing projects, among other proposals.

Congress will also welcome an unusually large freshman class, including many Democrats elected in Republican-leaning states and districts. As of Thursday, Democrats had already flipped seven Senate seats, including five in states Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024. Democrats may also pick up still-undecided Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska, both of which Trump won handily in 2024.

Elections in the U.S. House of Representatives followed a similar pattern, with many Democrats winning in districts that Trump carried handily two years ago. Representing Republican-leaning constituencies could push many of these new members toward a bipartisan agenda, and housing offers a rare opportunity for common ground.

“I think you have a lot of new members coming in who will want to quickly show that they’re being productive and addressing what they ran on,” Winkler said, striking an optimistic tone. “The passage of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act in this Congress shows us that there is common ground on housing policy, and we now also have a model for how to get legislation enacted into law.”

The new Congress will be sworn in on January 3. Until then, Congress will be in a “lame duck” period. Ken Wingert, Chief Advocacy Officer at the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), wrote in a post-election analysis that Congress will likely begin debating the bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) during the lame duck session, offering a look at another potential federal housing bill.

BAAJA would streamline federal permitting and environmental reviews, lower land development costs and cut down on project delays that prolong the time it takes to secure federal approvals. NAHB argues the reforms could bring more affordable lots to market, accelerate multifamily development and lower costs for projects using federal housing financing and grants.

For his part, James Talarico, the Senator-elect from Texas, signaled during a Wednesday interview on Fox News that he is willing to work with Trump on several issues, including housing affordability.

“I also want to work with the President on housing. He’s a builder, and we need to cut the red tape, the regulations that sometimes my party has been guilty of, so that we can build millions of new homes in this country,” Talarico said.

Trump has also voiced a conciliatory tone since the election, signaling that he is open to working with a Democratic-controlled Congress on bipartisan legislation. Whether that holds true on housing or other critical areas remains to be seen.

“Democrats are expected to focus on increased funding for affordable housing programs, a greater emphasis on workforce training, and limits on President Trump’s tariff and immigration policies that have impacted new construction. At the same time, the Trump administration is expected to continue to pursue an agenda of deregulation that will help spur new housing supply,” Wingert wrote.

Winkler argued that federal funding and budget negotiations could become a major source of both bipartisan agreement and conflict in the next Congress, even if lawmakers can find common ground on housing policy itself.

The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act requires separate congressional appropriations to fund many of about a dozen newly enacted programs. Examples include the USDA rural housing preservation and rental assistance initiatives. Because of ROAD’s popularity, Congress could widely support appropriating funding for these programs.

“None of [the programs] have funding attached, so it will be a clear priority heading into next year if they want any of those grant programs to exist and actually work in practice,” Winkler explained.

However, disagreements over how to fund affordable housing programs and broader federal spending priorities could create fissures between Democrats and Republicans. Democrats will likely prioritize more funding for affordable housing and homelessness programs. They may also pursue oversight of the administration’s spending, particularly whether the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and other agencies are actually distributing housing grant money that Congress has already appropriated.

Winkler also expects scrutiny of HUD’s staffing reductions, which have reportedly cut the agency’s workforce by roughly 30%. The loss of experienced HUD employees could undermine the department’s ability to implement the ROAD to Housing Act’s numerous provisions. However, Congress has limited ability to force the administration to fund and hire more employees, and any legislation would likely still need presidential support.

Democratic leadership has already signaled that they will attempt to take on Trump’s tariff agenda once they assume power in January. It’s unclear, though, how successful that effort will be and if Trump will leverage executive powers to keep certain tariffs in place.

However, Democrats in Congress have already introduced multiple bills to exempt building materials from tariffs in a bid to lower housing costs, including the Housing Tariff Exclusion Act that was introduced earlier this year. NAHB threw its support behind that legislation.

Democrats will likely push for a similar policy of tariff exemptions over the next two years. And, for what it’s worth, the Build America Caucus, which has 21 Republican members, has called for exempting building materials from tariffs as part of its housing policy agenda. If a similar provision is included in a comprehensive follow-up housing bill, it could create a potential policy clash with the Trump administration.

Other policy issues, such as the impact of immigration enforcement on the construction labor pool or a renewed push to expand an already-passed institutional investor ban on purchasing single-family homes, could also create friction between Democrats and Republicans in Congress, and the Trump administration.

Still, bipartisan support is possible in certain areas, like streamlining regulations and funding the programs created by ROAD. However, even where bipartisan support exists, Democratic leadership will, in most cases, need the administration’s backing to turn its priorities into law.

“The president has the veto, so legislation moving forward does need buy-in from everybody,” Winkler said.

#5587. Treasury, IRS finalize new Opportunity Zone designations

Treasury and the IRS designated 6,576 census tracts as new Qualified Opportunity Zones under the Working Families Tax Cuts, effective Jan. 1, 2027, with a 10-year term and enhanced incentives for rural areas.  AI Summary

The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) designated 6,576 census tracts across all 50 states, territories and the District of Columbia as new Qualified Opportunity Zones, according to a Thursday announcement.

The action, which will take effect Jan. 1, 2027, will permanently renew the federal Opportunity Zone tax incentive and add enhanced benefits for investment in eligible rural communities. It also establishes a process to redesignate opportunity zones every 10 years, meaning that the newly announced map will remain in place through the end of 2036.

IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano, in a press release, said that the permanent extension and expansion of the program will “give states an opportunity to attract long-term investment into underserved, rural and economically distressed areas”, and that “the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most.”

Opportunity Zones, initially created as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, are designed to incentivize investment in economically disadvantaged communities by allowing investors, including builders and developers, to defer or reduce capital gains taxes when they invest in qualified projects.

For housing developers and homebuilders, the updated map and permanent extension of the incentive should provide more clarity on eligible locations and long-term planning for the next decade.

That certainty stems from changes made by the Working Families Tax Cuts, which President Trump signed into law in 2025.

The legislation made the Opportunity Zone program permanent, established enhanced tax incentives for rural communities and created a process to redesignate eligible census tracts every 10 years.

In an announcement, Treasury said that the Working Families Tax Cuts build on more than $110 billion in private-sector investment made in Opportunity Zones since the program was launched in 2017. The bill narrowed the pool of eligible zones from 8,764 and strengthened incentives for rural communities. Although urban areas will continue to represent a significant share of designated zones, the changes could encourage more investment in rural markets with limited access to housing capital.The changes complement a provision in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that allows the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to favor grant applications if their housing development is located in or primarily serves a designated Opportunity Zone. The aim of that provision is to spur more housing supply in economically distressed communities.

The program, which applies to both market-rate and below-market housing, is popular among residential developers. A 2025 Urban Institute analysis found that 64% of Opportunity Zone capital in Ohio went toward residential development, for example. And a separate 2025 analysis by the Economic Innovation Group concluded that the program roughly doubled housing supply in eligible zones.

#5585. Atlassian shares fall 17% as slower subscription growth forecast overshadows earnings beat

Shares in Atlassian Corp. fell more than 17% in after-hours trading today on a forecast for slower subscription growth from the Australian collaboration software company.

Its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results beat analyst estimates. The stock had nearly doubled between Atlassian’s August report and late October.

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, Atlassian reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.65, up from $1.04 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $1.772 billion, up 24% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.43 per share on revenue of $1.71 billion.

Most of the growth came from cloud, where revenue rose 31%, to $1.302 billion. Customers kept adding Jira and Confluence seats in the quarter, according to the shareholder letter, including in business teams well outside software development.

Growth in Data Center, the self-managed product line Atlassian will retire in March 2029, slowed to about 5%, leaving revenue there at $391 million. The company said those customers are expanding less as they plan their moves to the cloud.

Subscription annual recurring revenue came in at $6.812 billion at the end of September, up 22.5%. Remaining performance obligations jumped 44%, to $4.746 billion. Enterprise customers are behind that increase, according to the company, with deals getting larger and stretching over several years.

Atlassian made money on an unadjusted basis for the second quarter running, with net income of $91 million, or 35 cents per share. Chief Financial Officer James Chuong put that down to keeping costs in check while revenue grew. Free cash flow climbed to $463 million on strong collections, and Atlassian returned $581 million to shareholders through buybacks.

On the product side, more than 87% of enterprise cloud customers now use Rovo, the company’s artificial intelligence assistant. Upgrades to the Teamwork Collection bundle rose sevenfold from a year ago to more than 3,000 customers. Annual recurring revenue from the larger Service Collection bundle is now above $1 billion, spread across more than 70,000 customers.

Chief Executive Mike Cannon-Brookes used the earnings release to argue that enterprise AI has reached “an inflection point.” Model power alone no longer sets anyone apart, he said. Platforms that give people and AI agents shared context to work from will pull ahead by his account, and Atlassian has “never been better positioned” to be one of them.

For the second quarter, Atlassian expects revenue of $1.825 billion to $1.835 billion, a little ahead of the $1.82 billion analysts had forecast, with cloud revenue growth of about 27%.

Most of Atlassian’s fiscal 2027 targets edged higher in the update. The company now sees full-year revenue growth of about 13.75%, three-quarters of a point above its August forecast. Because customers pulled Data Center purchases into fiscal 2026 after the retirement announcement, this year’s revenue comparisons are tougher.

Total revenue growth should pick up again in fiscal 2028, Atlassian said. Investors sold the stock on a different number. The company expects subscription annual recurring revenue growth to slow to about 18.5% by fiscal year-end, down from the 22.5% it just reported.

#5582. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5581. Stanford Radiologist and AI Leader Curtis Langlotz, MD, PhD, Joins Raidium Strategic Advisory Board

Langlotz will advise on how AI-assisted radiology reporting is validated and built around radiologists; Raidium to host November 10 webinar on the use and future of AI in radiology

PARIS, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Raidium, an AI imaging company building tools for radiology and oncology imaging, today announced that Curtis Langlotz, MD, PhD, Professor of Radiology, Medicine, and Biomedical Data Science at Stanford University, has joined its strategic advisory board. Langlotz will advise Raidium on the clinical validation and responsible development of AI-assisted radiology reporting.

"The radiology report is how our work reaches patients and the clinicians who care for them, and AI has been transforming how reports are being written for a while," said Langlotz. "The important question now is how to build these tools so radiologists stay in control, can see how a draft was produced, and can trust what they sign. I'm glad to support the Raidium team as they work through those questions alongside practicing radiologists."

Dr. Langlotz has emphasized that trust in AI for radiology depends on validating the full system, including how models, clinical workflows and radiologist review work together, rather than measuring a single model in isolation. He will help Raidium apply that standard as it develops and evaluates its technology with clinical partners.

"Curtis has spent his career on the questions that matter most to us: how radiologists communicate what they find, and how AI can find its right place in the reading room," said Paul HÃ©rent, MD, PhD, Chief Medical Officer at Raidium. "His perspective will help us build our technology around the way radiologists actually work, with clinicians in control at every step. We're honored to welcome him to our strategic advisory board."

Langlotz joins Ludovic d'AprÃ©a, Strategic Advisor, who joined the board in October.

Raidium will host a webinar, "Usage and Perspectives of AI in Radiology," on Tuesday, November 10, at 8 a.m. CST. Dr. Langlotz will join the discussion. Registration is open at https://app.livestorm.co/raidium/usage-and-perspective-of-ai-in-radiology.

About Curtis Langlotz, MD, PhDDr. Langlotz is Professor of Radiology, Medicine, and Biomedical Data Science, and Senior Associate Vice Provost for Research at Stanford University. His laboratory develops machine learning methods to improve the accuracy and efficiency of medical image interpretation by detecting disease early and reducing medical errors. He also serves as Senior Fellow at Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence and Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence in Medicine and Imaging, which supports over 250 faculty at Stanford who pursue interdisciplinary machine learning research to improve clinical care.

About RaidiumRaidium is an AI-native radiology company building the tools that radiologists have been waiting for. Combining a world-class foundation model research lab with a unified, promptable AI viewer, Raidium automates complex radiology workflows from indication to final report while keeping the radiologist in control at every step. For oncology, the Raidium Read platform automates RECIST imaging endpoints for research and clinical trials use. The Curia foundation model demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across imaging tasks, with peer-reviewed publication forthcoming in Radiology AI. Raidium operates globally with offices in Paris, France and Silicon Valley, USA.

#5579. OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, an Astra model built to keep vulnerability research in scope

OpenAI Group PBC today released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for authorized vulnerability research.

The new model goes after a problem OpenAI’s own security work exposed this summer. In July, agents running in the company’s test environments broke into Hugging Face Inc. while pursuing an assigned task. GPT-6 Cyber was trained to stay inside the targets a researcher has authorized, and the safety test OpenAI built for the launch draws on that incident.

That test, ExploitGym Honeypot, gives the model a difficult assignment and surrounds it with supporting services that are deliberately easy to compromise. Attacking any of those services counts as a scope violation.

With no deployment safety instructions in place, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds in 0.07% of graded runs. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6-Cyber, did so 5.51% of the time. Adding the instructions brought GPT-6 Cyber’s observed rate to zero.

OpenAI rates the new model at Critical, the top cybersecurity tier in its Preparedness Framework and the same classification Astra received at its September launch. GPT-5.6-Cyber had been rated High. The company says GPT-6 Cyber beats Astra on most cyber tasks, and an early research campaign on Firefox turned up 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla Corp. rated high severity. Mozilla has since shipped fixes for many of them.

Irregular, an AI security lab named in the system card, put the gap with Astra closer, finding the two broadly comparable apart from stronger GPT-6 Cyber results on long multistep tasks. Neither model got past fully hardened targets in OpenAI’s own challenge set.

GPT-6 Cyber is the fourth cyber-specific model OpenAI has released this year. Like the first, GPT-5.4-Cyber, it sits behind an application process. Initial access is limited to a select group of approved customers in Daybreak Red, the tier of OpenAI’s Daybreak program meant for offensive-style work such as penetration testing and red teaming. Those customers reach the model through the company’s application programming interface and Codex, and API requests have to come from approved networks by default.

Google LLC also put vetted defenders first when it launched Gemini 4 Argon in September. A week later Anthropic PBC rebuilt its Cyber Verification Program around three access tiers.

OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber will reach all Daybreak Red customers over the coming weeks, and GPT-5.6-Cyber is now opening to every customer in the tier. Critical infrastructure defenders get a Daybreak Red group of their own. On the defensive side, the company is extending early Astra access through Daybreak Blue to more organizations and to individual security researchers.

#5577. Capital Group Global Equity Study: U.S. dividend growth across industries reaches Q3 record

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- U.S. companies distributed $180.7 billion in dividends to investors in Q3, with 96% increasing or maintaining their payouts, according to the latest Dividend Watch from Capital Group, the world's largest active fund manager1, and part of the Capital Group Global Equity Study2.

"The market's underlying sources of investor returns appear broader than the narrow group dominating the headlines," said David Unanue, Head of Asset Class Services at Capital Group. "While investors are understandably focused on the growth of AI, record dividend payments show that companies across a range of industries are generating cash and returning more of it to investors. For long-term active investors like Capital Group, that creates an opportunity to look across sectors and distinguish between companies that simply offer attractive payouts today and those with the underlying cash generation, earnings growth and financial flexibility to sustain them over time."

Global growth acceleratesGlobally, dividends reached a third-quarter record of $546 billion, increasing 7.5% on a core basis year over year. Financials were the largest contributor, accounting for approximately one-third of the increase, or $11 billion. General financial companies increased payouts by 17.6%, supported by strong capital markets, trading activity and fee income.

But financials were not the only source of growth. Mining and chemicals recorded the fastest sector increase, with payouts rising 21.7%, while technology dividends increased 10.9%. Mining and technology each contributed approximately one-sixth of the overall increase in global dividends.

2026 outlook improvesFollowing stronger-than-expected Q3 results, the study upgraded the 2026 global dividend forecast to a record $2.24 trillion. Core growth is now expected to reach 6.8%, up from the previous forecast of 6.0%, reflecting stronger underlying distributions and improved expectations for the final quarter.

Resilient earnings and healthy cash generation continue to support the outlook for investor distributions, although economic and geopolitical uncertainty and uneven growth across markets remain considerations heading into year-end.

Footnotes1 Source: Morningstar Direct as of June 30, 2026. This does not include money market funds, feeder funds or fund of funds.

#5576. Is Trump Media Selling Bitcoin? Democrats Prepare Crypto Probe

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The company sent 4,259 BTC in two transactions, according to blockchain data tracked by Arkham. The coins came from wallets labeled as collateral for convertible notes, adding another layer of uncertainty around the Trump Media Bitcoin transfer.

The timing is difficult to ignore. Trump Media faces a potential $1 billion debt repayment deadline later this month, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are preparing to scrutinize Trump’s crypto businesses. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

A November 2 filing also disclosed that noteholders can require cash repayment on November 30. If all eligible holders exercise that option, the company could face approximately $1 billion in repayments.

Trump Media warned that refinancing or other measures might not be sufficient. In that scenario, the company could be forced to sell Bitcoin or other digital assets to meet its obligations.

This disclosure gives the Crypto.com transfer a potentially more serious explanation than routine custody management. The company may be positioning assets ahead of a major liquidity decision. Although the reason remains unconfirmed, Trump Media could be selling its Bitcoin.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The transfer also arrives as Democrats prepare to investigate Trump’s family crypto businesses after winning control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Incoming lawmakers have identified World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture, as a potential focus. Investigators are expected to examine foreign investment, business profits, and possible conflicts of interest involving the administration’s crypto dealings.

JUST IN: 🇺🇸 Democrats plan to investigate crypto industry's financial ties to President Trump and his family, Bloomberg reports. pic.twitter.com/KGF41xeknO

Senator Elizabeth Warren has pledged scrutiny of Trump’s crypto business relationships, while Representative Robert Garcia, expected to lead House Oversight, warned Trump-linked interests to prepare for investigations.

Democrats are expected to gain subpoena power when the new Congress begins in January. Reuters previously reported that investigations into Trump family businesses could begin as early as February.

The current political environment could complicate the outlook for Trump-linked companies. Congressional scrutiny may increase pressure on financial relationships, crypto holdings, and business operations connected to the president’s family.

So, is Trump Media selling its Bitcoin? There’s no clarity as of now, but a confirmed sale would raise questions if Trump Media is reducing its crypto treasury to meet financial obligations.

The next major date is November 30, when noteholders can exercise their repayment option. Investors will also be watching if the Bitcoin remains at Crypto.com, moves again, or appears in transactions that indicate an actual sale.

#5574. Cloudflare shares surge as revenue growth accelerates to 39% and outlook rises

Shares of Cloudflare Inc. jumped more than 14% in late trading today after the connectivity cloud company smashed third-quarter expectations and lifted its full-year outlook well above what Wall Street had been modeling.

The gain more than wiped out an 8% fall in the stock during the regular session.

For the quarter ended on Sept. 30, Cloudflare reported adjusted earnings per share of 38 cents, up from 27 cents in the same quarter of 2025, on revenue of $782.5 million, up 39% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 34 cents per share on revenue of $736.8 million.

Revenue growth hit its fastest pace in nearly four years as the annualized run rate crossed $3 billion. Current remaining performance obligations rose 37% from a year earlier. The adjusted operating margin also improved, to 17.5% from 15.3%, after shrinking year-over-year in each of the two prior quarters.

Because stock-based compensation ran to $174.1 million, Cloudflare still lost $34.1 million on an unadjusted basis, compared with a $1.3 million loss a year earlier. Another $11 million went to restructuring from the roughly 1,100 job cuts announced in May. Free cash flow slipped to 10% of revenue from 13% a year ago.

On the product side, short-lived blocking rules that write themselves during a live attack are the core of Adaptive Intelligence, which Cloudflare added to its Bot Management product in late August. AI agents got tools of their own earlier in the month through Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay, which give an agent an identity handle and will let it pay for services from a stablecoin balance. Federal agencies can now put more sensitive workloads on Cloudflare for Government, which reached FedRAMP High status in August.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Matthew Prince called the period “Cloudflare’s best quarter ever” in the earnings release. Cloudflare has built the development platform for the AI-powered internet, and organizations of every size keep turning to it for protection as digital threats escalate, he said. Prince added that the business has “found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth.”

Cloudflare also named Christian Smith president of revenue today, with responsibility for worldwide sales and revenue operations. He replaces Mark Anderson, who had already said he would retire from the full-time role at year-end. Smith previously ran sales at Splunk Inc. as chief revenue officer.

For the fourth quarter, Cloudflare expects adjusted earnings of 43 cents per share on revenue of $845 million to $846 million. Analysts had forecast 38 cents per share on revenue of $798.2 million.

Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, about $97 million above the midpoint of the range it gave in August. Analysts had been looking for $2.87 billion in revenue and $1.26 in adjusted earnings per share for the year, and the company is now guiding to $1.35.

#5573. Hanyang University Researchers Gain Control Over Where Semiconductor Crystals First Form

The method guides single crystals to begin growing in predefined central regions

GYEONGGI-DO, South Korea, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Controlling where crystals begin to form is a challenge in manufacturing two-dimensional semiconductors. Researchers from Hanyang University and collaborating institutions developed a method called etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation to direct crystal formation at specific locations, achieving over 99% single-crystal growth across 400 sites.

In semiconductor manufacturing, nucleation, when crystals first begin to form, determines where and how they grow. This is particularly important for two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors, which are promising for next-generation electronics. However, conventional area-selective growth methods cannot reliably control where crystals begin forming within designated regions, making it difficult to produce large single crystals and precisely aligned structures for electronic devices.

In a study published in Volume 658 of Nature on October 7, 2026, Professor Woo-Hee Kim from Hanyang University, Republic of Korea, and colleagues introduced a method called etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation (EF-SCN), which uses oxygen released from an oxide barrier to control where crystals begin to form.

Using this approach, the researchers grew molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), a two-dimensional semiconductor, on patterned substrates using metal-organic chemical vapor deposition. They surrounded each designated growth region with a hafnium oxide (HfO2) barrier that releases oxygen when heated to 750Â°C. The oxygen etches the material near the pattern boundaries, suppressing nucleation in these areas and favoring the formation of a single crystal at the center. As growth continues, the crystal expands outwards to form a larger single-crystal region.

The researchers demonstrated consistent, centrally located nucleation across patterned arrays. As the crystals grew, they filled their designated regions, forming single-crystal domains several micrometers across.

The researchers also modified the method to allow crystal growth at lower temperatures by replacing HfO2 with zirconium dioxide, which has a lower crystallization temperature and serves as an alternative etching-flux barrier. This allowed them to grow uniform, centrally nucleated triangular single-crystal MoSâ domains at temperatures as low as 430Â°C.

The researchers further investigated how growth conditions affect crystal formation. They found that the flow rate of diethyl sulfide, which supplies sulfur, primarily controls the number of nuclei that form. Too little can prevent nucleation, while too much can produce multiple crystals. The molybdenum precursor flow rate affects how far the crystals grow. By adjusting these conditions and the pattern dimensions, the researchers produced large crystals and line-shaped channels suitable for transistor integration.

The researchers produced crystals approximately 8 micrometers across and single-crystal films filling 10-micrometre growth regions. Across a 2-centimetre substrate, the method achieved a single-crystal yield exceeding 99%.

"To assess the electronic properties of these crystals, our team fabricated field-effect transistors using the MoS2 grown via our EF-SCN method," says Prof. Kim. The devices achieved a field-effect mobility of up to 117 cm2 V-1s-1. They integrated four transistors within a single crystal, with just 7.8% variation in electron mobility, demonstrating the potential to build denser electronic circuits with more consistent performance.

These findings establish EF-SCN as a method for controlling where crystals form, how they grow, and how they can be incorporated into electronic devices.

"This approach goes beyond conventional area-selective growth and enables highly reproducible single-crystal growth and provides a general framework for programming nucleation position, crystal geometry and subsequent device integration," says Prof. Kim.

Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux

#5572. FinThrive Appoints Sam Meckey as Chief Executive Officer

Experienced healthcare technology and operations executive to lead FinThrive's next chapter of innovation, operational excellence and growth

CEO Hemant Goel to retire and continue serving on the Board of Directors

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FinThrive, Inc., a leading healthcare revenue management software-as-a-service (SaaS) provider, backed by Clearlake Capital Group, L.P., today announced the appointment of Sam Meckey as Chief Executive Officer. Meckey will also join FinThrive's Board of Directors. He succeeds Hemant Goel, who is retiring after serving more than five years as President and CEO.

Meckey brings over 25 years of experience leading healthcare technology, software, and technology-enabled services organizations through growth, innovation, and operational transformation. He previously served as President of WestCX, part of West Technology Group, a provider of AI-native communication solutions for regulated industries. While at WestCX, Meckey led the integration of TeleVox and Mosaicx, launched WestCX Orchestrateâ¢, an AI-native customer engagement platform, and guided the business through its successful sale to Harris Healthcare.

As healthcare organizations face increasing financial pressure, administrative complexity, and the need to modernize fragmented technology environments, FinThrive is focused on advancing its integrated, end-to-end revenue cycle management platform. The company's broad technology capabilities, deep healthcare expertise, and established customer relationships are designed to help providers simplify operations, improve financial performance, and strive to realize greater value from automation, data, and artificial intelligence.

"I joined FinThrive because I believe in its mission and the opportunity ahead," said Meckey. "Providers are being asked to do more with less, and FinThrive is well positioned to help them. I'm excited to work closely with our team and our customers to accelerate innovation, harness the potential of AI and automation, and translate our capabilities into measurable results. Meckey also spent 14 years at Optum, ultimately serving as President of Optum Global Solutions, where he oversaw a global operations and technology services organization of more than 35,000 employees across the United States, India, the Philippines and Brazil. Earlier in his career, he served as a pilot and officer in the U.S. Navy. Meckey holds a Bachelor of Science in Economics from the United States Naval Academy, and a Master of Business Administration from Harvard Business School.

Goel is retiring after more than five years leading FinThrive as President and Chief Executive Officer and over 40 years of successful contributions to healthcare information technology. During his tenure at FinThrive, he helped advance the company's vision of delivering an integrated, end-to-end RCM technology platform to healthcare organizations. He will continue to serve on FinThrive's Board of Directors and work closely with Meckey to ensure a seamless transition.

"It has been a privilege to lead FinThrive for more than five years and to work alongside our talented colleagues and customers," said Goel. "I remain confident in our vision and the growing opportunity to help healthcare organizations consolidate technology, improve efficiency, and strengthen financial performance. Sam brings deep healthcare experience, a strong operating track record, and a commitment to innovation and customer outcomes. I am confident he is well positioned to lead FinThrive forward."

"Sam is an accomplished healthcare technology leader with a proven ability to drive operational transformation, accelerate innovation, and deliver results for customers," said Paul Huber, Partner and Managing Director at Clearlake. "His experience leading complex organizations at Optum and EXL, combined with his recent work advancing AI-enabled solutions at WestCX, makes him well suited to lead FinThrive's next chapter. We see significant opportunity to build on FinThrive's integrated platform, deepen customer partnerships, and drive sustainable growth. We also thank Hemant for his leadership and contributions to the Company."
